A Long Cloud on Mars Explanation: What’s causing this unusually long cloud on Mars ? Known as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC) and first recorded by NASA’s Viking Orbiter 2 in 1977, the strange cloud has been imaged in greater detail more recently by ESA ’s robotic Mars Express spacecraft. The featured image is from 2018. The cloud forms only during spring and summer seasons and then only during morning hours. Made of water-ice, the most familiar process that causes cloud crystals to form around bits of dust would fail due to the thinness and lack of dust high in the Martian atmosphere . Leading speculation holds that dust is not involved. After the cloud forms near the volcano Arsia Mons , wind blows the cloud downstream — creating a tail that can extend over 1500 kilometers. Efforts to better understand AMEC s will continue, an understanding that may bolster a more complete view of cloud formation on Earth . article.description: El telescopio espacial Euclid de la Agencia Espacial Europea ha descubierto su primer cometa previamente desconocido, en imágenes tomadas entre el 16 y el 24 de septiembre de 2026.
article.explanation:
TITULAR: Euclid descubre nuevo cometa
CATEGORIA: espacio

El telescopio espacial Euclid de la ESA ha logrado un hito inesperado al detectar su primer cometa previamente desconocido, denominado C/2026 S1 (Euclid). El hallazgo se produjo en imágenes capturadas entre el 16 y 24 de septiembre de 2026, mediante un software especializado en identificar objetos en movimiento desarrollado en la Universidad de Helsinki.

El cuerpo celeste se ubica a unos 1.300 millones de kilómetros de la Tierra, en una órbita que tardará miles de años en completarse. Aunque la misión principal de Euclid es mapear galaxias lejanas para estudiar la materia oscura, este descubrimiento demuestra su capacidad para detectar objetos del sistema solar mientras están lejos del Sol.

Como consecuencia, este éxito valida los protocolos de alerta temprana para la comunidad astronómica internacional. Además, permite a los científicos identificar y eliminar el "ruido" o rastro de luz que estos objetos generan en las imágenes, garantizando la precisión en la cartografía del universo profundo. El proceso servirá también como un caso de prueba para coordinar futuras misiones, como el Comet Interceptor.

TITULAR: Científicos descubren un sistema volcánico oculto de 100 millones de años
CATEGORIA: sismos

Un equipo internacional, liderado por la Universidad Técnica de Estambul, identificó un sistema volcánico previamente desconocido en el noroeste de Irán. Denominado Arco Magmático Continental de Azerbaiyán, este hallazgo revela un capítulo perdido de la historia geológica regional ocurrido hace unos 100 millones de años, durante el Cretácico Superior.

La investigación, publicada en *Geoscience Frontiers*, determinó que el sistema estuvo activo específicamente entre 101 y 97 millones de años atrás. Los científicos utilizaron técnicas avanzadas, como la geocronología de circones y análisis geoquímicos en rocas de la falla Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz, para confirmar que el magma se generó por el hundimiento de una placa tectónica bajo la corteza continental.

El descubrimiento es relevante porque este arco permaneció oculto debido a la eros

article.description: Un misterio de décadas bajo el Mar del Norte finalmente ha sido resuelto. Los científicos han confirmado que el Cráter Silverpit, enterrado a 700 metros debajo del lecho marino, fue creado cuando un asteroide de 160 metros de ancho chocó contra la Tierra hace aproximadamente entre 43 y 46 millones de años. La violenta colisión lanzó una cortina de roca y agua de 1.5 kilómetros hacia el aire y provocó un tsunami de más de 100 metros de altura.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Un asteroide masivo impactó en el Mar del Norte y desató un tsunami de 330 pies**

Un equipo de investigadores liderado por el Dr. Uisdean Nicholson de la Universidad Heriot-Watt en Edimburgo ha confirmado que un asteroide de aproximadamente 160 metros de ancho impactó en el Mar del Norte hace entre 43 y 46 millones de años, creando el cráter Silverpit. Este evento generó un tsunami que alcanzó más de 100 metros de altura, equivalente a un edificio de más de 30 pisos.

El cráter, que se encuentra a unos 700 metros bajo el lecho marino, fue descubierto en 2002, pero su origen había sido objeto de debate durante más de dos décadas. Algunos geólogos sostenían que su formación se debía a procesos geológicos, mientras que otros defendían la hipótesis del impacto. La reciente investigación, publicada en Nature Communications, combina imágenes sísmicas avanzadas y análisis de muestras de roca, revelando minerales que solo se forman bajo presiones extremas.

Los modelos numéricos sugieren que el impacto desplazó grandes cantidades de roca y agua, creando una cortina de escombros que generó el tsunami. Este descubrimiento no solo resuelve una controversia científica, sino que también ofrece una oportunidad única para estudiar los efectos de impactos de alta velocidad en la geología terrestre.

article.description: En esta Imagen del Mes del Telescopio Espacial James Webb de la NASA/ESA, visitamos un turbulento caldero de formación estelar para ver qué se está gestando dentro de densos cúmulos de gas. Esta es una región de formación estelar llamada LHA 120-N 159, o simplemente N159, ubicada a 161 000 años luz de distancia en la Nube Magallánica Grande (LMC), una de las galaxias satélites que orbitan la galaxia Vía Láctea. Esta imagen abarca aproximadamente 230 años luz de ancho.
article.explanation:
**Estrellas gestándose en un caldero nebuloso**

La región de formación estelar LHA 120-N 159, ubicada a 161,000 años luz en la Nube de Magallanes, es un fascinante laboratorio cósmico. Observaciones recientes del Telescopio Espacial James Webb han revelado detalles sobre este entorno turbulento, donde nubes moleculares de hidrógeno frío colapsan bajo la gravedad para dar origen a nuevas estrellas.

En N159, se han identificado áreas de gas ionizado, conocidas como regiones H II, que son indicadores de actividad estelar. Estas regiones brillan intensamente debido a la radiación ultravioleta de estrellas masivas y calientes, que también moldean el gas circundante mediante vientos estelares. Las imágenes muestran filamentos oscuros de hidrógeno molecular que protegen a las estrellas jóvenes de la radiación intensa.

Además, los datos obtenidos han permitido a los astrónomos detectar estrellas extremadamente tenues y distinguir entre estrellas jóvenes y aquellas que ya han evolucionado. Se ha observado que la región occidental de N159 alberga una mayor concentración de objetos estelares jóvenes, sugiriendo que está en una fase más temprana de formación. Este entorno único ofrece una oportunidad invaluable para estudiar la evolución de nubes moleculares y la formación estelar en condiciones similares a las del universo primitivo.

**TITULAR: El Hubble de la NASA marca el camino para el telescopio espacial Roman**

El telescopio espacial Hubble de la NASA ha capturado imágenes que servirán como base para las futuras observaciones del telescopio Nancy Grace Roman, programado para su lanzamiento en 2027. En una imagen reciente, tomada el 22 de octubre de 2026, se observa una galaxia espiral con un lente gravitacional en la esquina inferior derecha, lo que permite a los astrónomos estudiar las distorsiones gravitacionales y su relación con la materia oscura.

Estas imágenes son parte de una serie de observaciones que Hubble ha realizado para preparar el terreno para el Roman, que se enfocará en investigar la estructura del universo y la naturaleza de la materia oscura. Los científicos esperan que la colaboración entre ambos telescopios proporcione una visión más completa del cosmos, permitiendo avances significativos en la comprensión de fenómenos astronómicos.

El telescopio Roman, con su capacidad para observar grandes áreas del cielo, complementará las observaciones detalladas de Hubble, ofreciendo nuevas oportunidades para explorar el universo y responder preguntas fundamentales sobre su composición y evolución.

**TITULAR: El tsunami monstruoso de Alaska lanzó agua 1.580 pies montaña arriba**

El 9 de agosto de 2025, un deslizamiento de tierra en Alaska provocó el segundo tsunami más alto registrado en la historia, alcanzando una altura de 1.580 pies (481 metros) en el fiordo de Tracy Arm. El evento ocurrió doce horas después de que los pasajeros del crucero Hanse Explorer finalizaran su visita al glaciar South Sawyer. A las 5 de la mañana, el deslizamiento de tierra, causado por la combinación de la rápida pérdida de hielo y las intensas precipitaciones, colapsó en el fiordo, generando olas devastadoras que despojaron las paredes del fiordo hasta dejar la roca desnuda.

Este fenómeno no es aislado; en los últimos años, se ha observado un patrón de deslizamientos de tierra en las terminaciones de glaciares en retroceso en la costa de Alaska. Investigadores del Alaska Earthquake Center advierten que la inestabilidad de estas montañas se agrava con el deshielo. Aunque no hubo barcos en la cercanía durante el evento, las consecuencias han llevado a algunas líneas de cruceros a evitar Tracy Arm.

Los científicos sugieren que un sistema de alerta podría haber mitigado el riesgo, proporcionando advertencias a las embarcaciones y comunidades cercanas. Sin embargo, actualmente no existe un sistema de monitoreo de deslizamientos a esta escala en Estados Unidos, lo que resalta la necesidad de mejorar la vigilancia geofísica y meteorológica en estas áreas vulnerables.

Cuando se miden con precisión la fuerza y la respuesta completas, las ondulaciones en el pico y los contactos separados siguen siendo entradas conocidas. La forma de la fuerza cambia la excitación, pero no invalida inherentemente el registro. La adecuación depende de la precisión de la medición, el ancho de banda, la relación señal-ruido y la cobertura del objetivo de la prueba. Antecedentes: Lo que realmente mide el martillo Las pruebas con martillo apoyan el análisis modal [2–4] y pueden preceder a las pruebas de pyroshock [6]. La Figura 1 compara un medio seno, ondulaciones de contacto mantenido y contactos separados. Durante un intervalo de fuerza cero, la estructura continúa vibrando; el re-contacto actúa sobre esa vibración. Si un modelo exacto y un artículo de prueba reciben la misma fuerza y condiciones iniciales, la unicidad da respuestas idénticas para cada historia medida acotada. Un modelo aproximado puede mostrar diferentes errores a medida que las entradas excitan diferentes frecuencias, amplitudes o estados no lineales. An approximate model can show different errors as inputs excite different frequencies, amplitudes, or nonlinear states. See [1] for the exact-model derivation. Its appearance alone cannot establish adequate excitation. Analysis: Spectral Content Is Determined by the Measured Force History Figure 3 normalizes each spectrum to its own DC value. Crest rippling adds content and can fill half-sine notches. Timing between separated contacts creates deterministic interference. For adequacy, inspect the unnormalized measured spectrum and response signal-to-noise ratio. **TITULAR: NASA y NOAA monitorean el agujero de ozono antártico de 2026**

El agujero de ozono antártico de 2026 ha sido objeto de seguimiento por parte de la NASA y la Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica (NOAA), quienes informaron que, a pesar de un aumento en su tamaño, la capa de ozono sigue en camino hacia una recuperación a largo plazo. Este agujero, que se formó entre el 7 de septiembre y el 13 de octubre, alcanzó una extensión promedio de aproximadamente 9.6 millones de millas cuadradas (25 millones de kilómetros cuadrados), siendo el séptimo más grande en 48 años de monitoreo.

El 18 de septiembre, el agujero alcanzó su máxima extensión diaria, cubriendo 10.5 millones de millas cuadradas (27.1 millones de kilómetros cuadrados). Aunque su tamaño es considerable, no fue tan profundo como los agujeros más grandes registrados en décadas anteriores. La investigación indica que un vórtice polar inusualmente fuerte contribuyó a la prolongación de la depleción de ozono en la región.

Los científicos destacan que los controles establecidos por el Protocolo de Montreal en 1987 han sido efectivos, logrando una disminución de aproximadamente un tercio en los niveles de cloro en la estratosfera antártica desde los años 80. Se estima que la recuperación completa del agujero podría ocurrir para la década de 2070.

article.source_body: 4 min read NASA, NOAA Track 2026 Antarctic Ozone Hole Earth’s protective ozone layer remains on track for long-term recovery, despite atmospheric conditions that contributed to a larger Antarctic ozone hole in 2026, NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reported. The ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring, but was not as deep as other large holes on record. From Sept. 7 to Oct. 13, peak ozone depletion season, the average extent of the hole covered about 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). Scientists continually track the amount of ozone in the stratosphere because it acts as the Earth’s sunscreen that helps shield life from harmful solar radiation. This is distinct from ground level ozone, which is an air pollutant commonly resulting from human activities. This data visualization shows the area and shape of the ozone hole on September 18, 2026, the day of its annual maximum extent. Scientists define the ozone hole as the area in which ozone concentrations drop below the historical threshold of 220 Dobson units. NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin “The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.” The ozone hole reached its greatest one-day extent for the year on Sept. 18 at 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). For comparison, the largest ozone hole observed since monitoring began reached its maximum extent in September 2000. “The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their peak in 2000,” Newman said. The Antarctic polar vortex helps create the cold conditions that allow chlorine and bromine from human-made compounds to deplete stratospheric ozone. “The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically propagate up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. “That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.” Despite its relatively large area, this year’s ozone hole was not as deep as the record ozone holes observed in previous decades. Using balloon-borne instruments from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory, NOAA scientists found that ozone concentrations directly overhead reached their lowest value for the year — 105 Dobson units — on Oct. 17. The Dobson unit is the standard measurement used to express ozone concentration. The lowest value recorded over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006. In addition to NOAA’s balloon- and ground-based observations, satellite data has been integral to monitoring the health of Earth’s protective ozone layer since 1979. Instruments aboard NASA’s Aura satellite, the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, jointly operated by NASA and NOAA, all contributed to the report. NOAA Corps LT Michael Doneghey, the South Pole observatory station lead, holds a weather balloon while NOAA Station Technician Luke Longren carries a package containing an ozonesonde — an airborne instrument that measures ozone levels — just prior to launch on October 18, 2026. Amentum/Tommy Jensen. With permission. NASA and NOAA scientists said that the ongoing monitoring shows that controls established by the Montreal Protocol in 1987 continue to drive long-term recovery of stratospheric ozone. As part of that agreement, countries committed to replacing ozone-depleting substances with less-harmful alternatives. From their peak, chlorine levels in the Antarctic stratosphere derived from ozone-depleting substances have since declined by about a third relative to 1980s levels, said Stephen Montzka, senior scientist of the NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory. Chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once widely used in consumer goods like refrigerators, air conditioners, and building insulation. They can linger in the atmosphere or leach out of old products and landfills for many decades. As those legacy compounds break down, scientists estimate that the ozone hole will recover by the 2070s. **TITULAR: El instrumento CASALS de la NASA cierra brechas en los mapas 3D de la superficie de la Tierra**

Un equipo de investigadores del Centro de Vuelo Espacial Goddard de la NASA ha desarrollado el Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS), un innovador instrumento que promete revolucionar la forma en que se mapea la superficie terrestre. Este dispositivo combina aprendizaje automático con un lidar ultra compacto para eliminar los espacios vacíos que dejan los métodos tradicionales de medición.

CASALS utiliza un láser de pulso rápido que opera a 1040 nanómetros, capaz de generar un barrido continuo de la superficie terrestre, en lugar de depender de espejos mecánicos. Esta técnica permite obtener representaciones topográficas tridimensionales con una resolución horizontal de 22 centímetros, lo que facilita la identificación de detalles como ramas individuales de árboles y cambios sutiles en la elevación del terreno.

En noviembre de 2024, un prototipo de CASALS voló a bordo de un avión B200 King Air, logrando recopilar datos científicos de alta calidad en su primera campaña. Los investigadores planean realizar mejoras antes de su transición a una versión espacial, con el objetivo de que CASALS se convierta en el primer lidar espacial capaz de mapear la Tierra de manera continua, proporcionando una visión más completa de nuestro planeta en constante cambio.

article.original_title: NASA’s CASALS Instrument Bridges Gaps in 3D Maps of Earth’s Surface
article.source_body: Explore This Section Overview Technology Programs Technology Highlights Workshops and Events Publications From orbit, today’s space-based laser instruments measure Earth’s forests and terrain one narrow line at a time. Between those lines are enormous gaps that include millions of acres of land scientists never directly measure. NASA’s CASALS instrument will blend machine learning with an ultra-compact lidar instrument to adaptively ‘sweep’ large swaths of Earth’s surface. This new capability for space-based remote sensors allows CASALS to create truly three-dimensional (3D) topographical renderings. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Video from a CASALS flight over the Great Cypress Swamp in Delaware on Nov. 12, 2024, showing tree canopy tops in green, the ground in purple, and near-ground vegetation in blue. Credit: NASA A team of researchers at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) has developed a new instrument designed to eliminate blind spots between lines of lidar data on the Earth’s surface. Built with support from NASA’s Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO), the Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS) could help researchers map the features of Earth’s surface with unprecedented detail. Rather than mechanically steering a laser with moving mirrors, CASALS steers light using wavelength itself, generating a continuous, 3D swath of the ground below. John Yorks, a physical research scientist at GSFC and Principal Investigator for CASALS, explained that the instrument features a novel transmitter and optical grating system that manipulates laser pulses without heavy, failure-prone motorized mirrors. Instead, CASALS uses a fast-pulsing, tunable “seed” laser centered at 1040 nanometers, rapidly cycling through 256 unique wavelengths as it pulses through an optical component with a microscopic pattern of ridges called a transmission grating. At this point, the physics of diffraction takes over. Because light bends at slightly different angles depending on its exact wavelength, the grating naturally “steers” each of the 256 pulses into a distinct position across the flight path. This non-mechanical approach paints a continuous 3D swath of the ground. Not only does this eliminate the large unmapped gaps left between the isolated tracks of legacy spaceborne lidars, but stripping away moving parts drastically reduces the instrument’s size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements. This makes it more reliable for the harsh environment of space. Another key innovation within CASALS is its detector array. This component features a uniquely high Quantum Efficiency (QE), a variable that describes how effectively a detector converts incoming light (photons) into an electrical signal. CASALS operates at 80% QE. This means CASALS wastes almost none of the light that makes it back to the sensor. With QE that high, CASALS can detect much weaker return signals, allowing it to collect useful measurements from darker surfaces or through denser vegetation. This technology isn’t limited to a laboratory environment. In November 2024, an airborne CASALS prototype flew aboard NASA’s B200 King Air aircraft. The instrument produced science-quality datasets on its first campaign, exceeding the team’s expectations. “I’m very impressed with Guang Yang, Jeffrey Chen, and all our engineers, and how well CASALS performed. This worked really well from the first time we flew it, which is pretty impressive,” said Yorks. Flying at an altitude of roughly five kilometers, CASALS can distinguish individual tree branches and subtle changes in ground elevation, thanks to its 22-centimeter horizontal resolution. “We’re able to see really fine details of vegetation structure and changes in the topography of the surface,” Yorks said. The team aims to fly CASALS again as part of the Airborne Surface, Cryosphere, Ecosystem, and Nearshore Topography (ASCENT) campaign, scheduled for summer 2027. But there’s more work to do to prepare the technology for space. The team plans to make several improvements to CASALS before creating a space-ready prototype. Specifically, they’re widening the instrument’s swath and adding onboard data processing software. Transitioning from a successful airborne prototype to a fully realized space mission is a challenge, but the CASALS team is up to the task. “The team’s really done a great job of sticking together and keeping on task and on schedule. We are being funded to optimize and improve the performance, and we’re also then looking at ways to take the technologies used in the airborne instrument and mature them and prepare them for a spaceborne version in the future,” said Yorks. If successful, CASALS could become the first spaceborne lidar capable of mapping Earth’s forests and terrain as continuous three-dimensional swaths rather than isolated profiles, giving scientists a dramatically more complete picture of our changing planet. **Los cuerpos humanos producen 2 mil millones de toneladas métricas de CO2 al año solo por mantenerse vivos.**

Un estudio liderado por la Universidad de Bath reveló que el metabolismo humano genera anualmente 2,05 mil millones de toneladas métricas de CO2. Esta cifra representa un aumento del 74% en comparación con 1985, cuando la producción estimada era de 1,18 mil millones.

La investigación, publicada en *The Lancet Planetary Health*, atribuye este incremento principalmente al crecimiento poblacional. Más del 60% del alza se debe a que hoy somos más personas en el planeta, y no a un cambio sustancial en la cantidad de gas que cada individuo exhala al convertir alimentos en energía.

Los expertos aclaran que este proceso biológico no impulsa el cambio climático. A diferencia de los combustibles fósiles, que liberan carbono atrapado por millones de años, el CO2 metabólico proviene de la dieta y ya forma parte del ciclo natural del carbono.

Contar con estas mediciones precisas permite a los científicos entender mejor el ciclo global del carbono

article.explanation: **TITULAR: El SR-1 Freedom de la NASA avanza con progresos en el módulo de energía nuclear** **CATEGORÍA: espacio** La NASA ha dado un paso significativo en el desarrollo del Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, el primer spacecraft que utilizará energía de fisión fuera de la órbita terrestre. Este ambicioso proyecto, anunciado durante el evento "Ignition", tiene como objetivo demostrar la propulsión eléctrica nuclear en el espacio profundo, con un lanzamiento programado para finales de 2028. El módulo de energía nuclear, ubicado en el extremo del brazo del SR-1, incluye un reactor que genera calor a través de la fisión nuclear y un sistema de conversión de energía que transforma ese calor en electricidad. Sierra Lobo Inc. será responsable del sistema de conversión de ciclo Brayton cerrado, esencial para la propulsión eléctrica del spacecraft. Este trabajo se enmarca dentro del contrato Space Flight Systems Development and Operations Contract III, otorgado en 2024. Además, el diseño del reactor está a cargo del Laboratorio Nacional de Idaho del Departamento de Energía, que asegura que se cumplan rigurosos estándares de seguridad. La misión SR-1 Freedom también llevará el proyecto SkyFall, que incluye tres helicópteros para Marte, destinados a recolectar datos científicos y explorar posibles fuentes de agua. Este avance marca un hito en la exploración espacial y el desarrollo de sistemas de energía nuclear para futuras misiones.

article.source_body: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Space Reactor-1 Freedom will be the first spacecraft ever to demonstrate fission power beyond Earth’s orbit, traveling to Mars to deliver a science payload called SkyFall. NASA/Alberto Bertolin Destined for Mars and beyond, NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will be humanity’s first fission-powered spacecraft to travel outside Earth’s orbit. Announced during NASA’s “ Ignition ” event, this mission will demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space, and progress is underway on its key element: the nuclear power module. To expedite development of the spacecraft, NASA and its partners have mutually agreed to key contract actions that will advance the SR‑1 Freedom mission. “These contract actions not only reduce technical risk and help us maintain momentum toward our 2028 launch, but they also strengthen collaboration across our partners,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “These actions keep SR‑1 Freedom on track and ensure we’re building the strongest possible foundation for NASA’s first fission‑powered voyage beyond Earth orbit while developing technology extensible to a vibrant space nuclear future.” Space Reactor-1 Freedom’s nuclear power module, located at the end of the spacecraft’s boom, consists of a reactor that generates heat through nuclear fission and a power conversion system that converts that heat into electricity to power systems and electric propulsion. NASA/Alberto Bertolin Sierra Lobo Inc. will provide the nuclear power module’s closed Brayton cycle power conversion system, which converts thermal energy from its fission reactor into electrical power needed for SR-1 Freedom’s nuclear electric propulsion demonstration. The work will be conducted under the Space Flight Systems Development and Operations Contract III, awarded in 2024 , to support spaceflight hardware design, development, testing, and operations at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland. The power conversion system will be integrated with the fission reactor, which is being designed and developed by the Department of Energy (DOE)’s Idaho National Laboratory to complete the nuclear power module. NASA and DOE incorporate thorough safety standards throughout the design and development of the SR-1 Freedom spacecraft, including interagency safety reviews, continuous oversight by a NASA chief safety officer, regulatory compliance, and a rigorous safety design process focusing on hazards, failure tolerance, and nuclear safety. In addition, the nuclear reactor portion of SR-1 Freedom will remain inactive until the spacecraft leaves Earth orbit. Launching in late 2028, SR‑1 Freedom will deliver the SkyFall science mission, a team of three Mars helicopters evolved from the Ingenuity design, to collect scientific data, demonstrate exploration zones, and identify potential water sources. The mission will pave the way for deep space exploration and next‑generation fission-powered systems designed to keep NASA’s Moon Base operating through periods of darkness and in locations where solar power alone is not sufficient. For information about SR-1 Freedom, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/space-reactor-1-freedom/

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: NASA Nombra a Troy Asher Director del Centro de Investigación de Vuelo Armstrong**

NASA ha designado a Troy Asher como el nuevo director del Armstrong Flight Research Center, ubicado en Edwards, California. Asher, un experimentado piloto de pruebas e ingeniero aeroespacial, había estado desempeñando el cargo de director interino desde marzo de este año. Jared Isaacman, administrador de NASA, destacó que Asher ha dedicado su carrera a expandir los límites del vuelo, tanto como piloto de aeronaves experimentales como líder de equipos en misiones complejas.

El Armstrong Flight Research Center es fundamental para la reconstrucción del portafolio de aviones X de NASA y para el avance de la investigación en vuelo. Asher supervisará las operaciones y el personal del centro, que juega un papel crucial en el desarrollo de nuevas tecnologías de aviación y en la realización de misiones científicas aéreas.

Antes de asumir el cargo de director interino, Asher fue director de Operaciones de Vuelo en Armstrong, donde gestionó a pilotos, ingenieros y una flota de aeronaves especializadas. Su trayectoria incluye una carrera de 24 años en la Fuerza Aérea de EE. UU., donde estableció 25 récords mundiales de velocidad volando el bombardero B-1B. Con su nombramiento, se espera que Asher impulse la innovación en la investigación aeroespacial y fortalezca las capacidades de NASA en este campo.
article.original_title: NASA Names Troy Asher Armstrong Flight Research Center Director
article.source_body: Photo of Troy Asher NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Troy Asher director of the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Asher, a veteran test pilot and aerospace engineer with decades of experience in flight research and operations, has served as the center’s acting director since March. “Troy has spent his career pushing the boundaries of flight, both at the controls of experimental aircraft and leading the teams that make these missions possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “He understands what it takes to turn ambitious ideas into successful flight tests, and his experience will be invaluable as Armstrong leads the way in rebuilding NASA’s X-plane portfolio, restoring our flight-test capabilities, and flying higher, farther, and faster than we have in decades.” “Flight testing demands a rare combination of technical excellence, operational judgment, and trust in the teams that make every mission possible,” said NASA Associate Administrator and Chief Engineer Amit Kshatriya. “Troy’s service to America, from his distinguished career as an Air Force test pilot to his leadership of some of NASA’s most challenging flight research missions, embodies those qualities. Few people better understand the art and discipline of flight testing, and he brings a deep understanding of both the aircraft and the teams behind every successful mission. As director, Troy will help us revolutionize how we develop, evaluate, and fly new technologies, strengthening the capabilities that keep NASA at the forefront of aerospace research.” Asher will oversee Armstrong’s workforce and operations, leading NASA’s efforts to advance flight research, aircraft operations, and the development of new aviation technologies. As NASA’s Flight Test and Aircraft Operations Center of Excellence, Armstrong plays a central role in the agency’s efforts to rebuild and expand its X-plane portfolio, pushing the boundaries of high-speed flight and developing experimental aircraft and technologies that will shape the future of aviation. The center also supports airborne science missions and flight research across the agency. Prior to becoming acting center director, Asher served as director of Flight Operations at Armstrong, overseeing the center’s pilots, engineers, maintainers, and fleet of specialized aircraft supporting aeronautics research and scientific missions around the world. Asher joined NASA in 2008 as a research test pilot and aerospace engineer. During his time as a NASA pilot, he conducted flight research aboard aircraft, including the F-15, F/A-18, Gulfstream III, and X-56A unmanned aircraft system. He served as the lead test pilot for the development of NASA’s Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA) and flew scientific research missions aboard the agency’s DC-8 aircraft, supporting airborne science campaigns around the globe. Before joining NASA, Asher completed a 24-year career in the U.S. Air Force, retiring as a lieutenant colonel. His military service included assignments as an instructor at the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School at Edwards Air Force Base, commander of the 419th Flight Test Squadron, and director of the Bomber Combined Test Force. In 2003, he set 25 world speed records flying the B-1B bomber. Asher earned a bachelor’s degree in astronautical engineering from the U.S. Air Force Academy and a master’s degree in mechanical engineering from California State University, Fresno. Asher succeeds Bradley Flick, who retired in March following nearly 40 years of NASA service. Established in 1946, Armstrong has been at the forefront of American flight research for eight decades, from the first supersonic flight aboard the Bell X-1 to today’s work advancing quiet supersonic flight through NASA’s X-59 aircraft. The center continues to push the boundaries of aviation while providing critical flight research and operational capabilities in support of NASA’s science, technology, and exploration missions. article.description: El Hubble de la NASA estudió 37 galaxias enanas cercanas y encontró que gran parte del oxígeno que esperaban ver está ausente.
article.explanation: **TITULAR: El Hubble de la NASA descubre caso de oxígeno perdido en galaxias enanas cercanas** El Telescopio Espacial Hubble de la NASA ha revelado un enigma en nuestro vecindario cósmico. En un estudio publicado el 2 de noviembre de 2026 en The Astrophysical Journal, investigadores analizaron 37 galaxias enanas cercanas y encontraron que gran parte del oxígeno que se esperaba observar está ausente. Estas galaxias, que contienen desde unos pocos miles hasta cientos de millones de estrellas, parecen retener solo una pequeña fracción del oxígeno producido por sus estrellas. Los científicos sugieren que el oxígeno, generado por las estrellas, ha sido expulsado de estas galaxias debido a vientos galácticos impulsados por supernovas. Grace Telford, co-investigadora y profesora asistente en la Universidad de Utah, explicó que la energía de estas explosiones es crucial para entender cómo el material se escapa hacia el espacio intergaláctico. El proyecto, denominado Galaxias que Pierden Oxígeno a Través de Vientos (GLOW), busca comprender la distribución del oxígeno en las galaxias y su papel en la evolución galáctica. Kristen Wingfield McQuinn, investigadora principal del GLOW, destacó que el oxígeno es un indicador clave para estudiar cómo las galaxias enriquecen el medio intergaláctico. Este hallazgo podría tener implicaciones significativas para nuestra comprensión de la formación y evolución de las galaxias en el universo.

Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, Hubble Heritage–ESA/Hubble Collaboration, Alessandra Aloisi (STScI, ESA) NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope just revealed a mystery in our cosmic neighborhood. In a paper published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies — small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars — and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing. Simulations predict that significantly more oxygen, a tracer of a wider set of heavy elements, should reside in these galaxies. So where did it go? “Oxygen is produced by stars, which are inside of galaxies. We know that the oxygen had to be inside of the galaxies at some point in the past, so the oxygen must have been ejected,” said co-investigator Grace Telford, assistant professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Utah. “And to do that, you need energy from massive stars and supernova explosions to drive material out of the host galaxies and into the space between galaxies.” Galactic winds unleashed by supernovae are apparently more effective at removing oxygen from low-mass galaxies than current models predict, according to the new study. The findings show that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. This is an image from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope of NGC 4449, one of the dwarf galaxies in the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) study. Researchers found that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by their stars. Image: NASA, ESA, Hubble Heritage–ESA/Hubble Collaboration, Alessandra Aloisi (STScI, ESA) In the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation, scientists traced the oxygen to understand how it is distributed inside stars, in the gas between stars, and in the space between galaxies. But, of all the elements in the galaxies, why study oxygen? Oxygen, the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium, is relatively easy to detect and measure, and its production is well understood — making it a reliable indicator of how chemical elements are distributed in a galaxy. “So, it’s really for practical reasons that we’ve chosen oxygen,” said Kristen Wingfield McQuinn, GLOW principal investigator and mission head of the Science Operations Center for NASA’s newly launched, panoramic Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, Maryland. She also is an associate professor at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey. “Oxygen is one of the primary elements formed by stars. Being able to trace how much oxygen gets made, and then how much is distributed inside and outside of galaxies, helps us understand galaxy evolution,” said McQuinn. “It also helps us learn where and how much galaxies are enriching the space between galaxies, called the intergalactic medium.” The study used archival optical imaging data from Hubble to resolve stellar populations and determine star-formation histories and compositions. Along with data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope as well as the ground-based Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array, the researchers analyzed 37 nearby dwarf galaxies to trace oxygen atoms produced by stars. The team wanted to understand how oxygen is distributed across the stars, gas, and dust in the galaxies. These dwarf galaxies were selected because their masses fall in the range where simulations and theory predict that an increasing amount of their oxygen will be expelled from the galaxies via supernovae explosions. These 37 galaxies also are all close enough for Hubble to resolve their individual stars. That’s not true for the vast majority of known dwarf galaxies, which are too far away for this kind of study. Although astronomers already suspected that galaxies expel a large fraction of oxygen and other heavy elements, an open question has been where these metals end up. A previous study from 2014 addressed this question for Milky Way-like, star-forming galaxies, finding that these galaxies lost a large fraction of their oxygen, some of which is found in the diffuse haloes of gas surrounding galaxies outside their disks, called the circumgalactic medium. In the GLOW study, McQuinn and her team extended this research to low-mass galaxies across a wide range of masses and environments. While previous teams have measured oxygen in the circumgalactic medium of dwarf galaxies, it is still unclear if most of the missing oxygen is in this region, or if it has been completely ejected from the galaxy’s surroundings. In the future, McQuinn hopes to study even lower-mass galaxies in the nearby universe. She has an approved program to use the Roman Space Telescope to find these faint and tiny systems across a wide swath of sky. Once she’s identified these galaxies, McQuinn hopes to use Hubble and NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope to get deeper observations of their stars. This would allow her to reconstruct the galaxies’ histories to understand how they formed stars across cosmic time. Telford’s future work involves using Hubble to zoom in on the individual, massive stars that produce oxygen and eject it from their host galaxies. She’s using some of the nearby GLOW targets to get very detailed observations to characterize how the massive stars are different in these small galaxies. The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for over three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA. Vegetation color is depicted on a spectrum ranging from dark green to light yellow to dark red. The largest patches of red vegetation appear in Alaska, northern Canada, Mongolia, and Russia. Smaller patches of red are visible in Australia. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A similar global map depicts the redness of vegetation from October 5 to 11. The reddest areas have shifted equatorward, with more color visible in the Mid-Atlantic, the U.S. Southeast, southern Russia, China, and Mongolia. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin September 29 to October 4 October 5 to 11 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Image Details These maps show the redness of vegetation as measured by the OCI (Ocean Color Instrument) on the PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite in September and October 2026. Red foliage appears to peak in New England, northern Canada, and northern Russia from September 29 to October 4, then spreads southward into the Mid-Atlantic, Mongolia, and northern China from October 5 to 11 (right). The Japanese tradition of momijigari , or “red leaf hunting,” stretches back more than a millennium, as evidenced by ancient poems describing journeys to admire fall foliage. In America, mentions of foliage trips began appearing in the historical record in the 19 th century, around the time artists and poets such as Frederic Church and Emily Dickinson celebrated autumn color in depictions of the Northeast. Modern-day leaf peepers have a new way to track and savor the seasonal phenomenon. The hyperspectral OCI (Ocean Color Instrument) on NASA’s PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite observes the planet’s oceans and vegetation daily at 286 spectral bands . Among this array are a few groups of wavelengths that allow scientists to track subtle changes in leaf pigments key to fall foliage displays, including anthocyanins (reds), carotenoids (yellows and oranges), and chlorophylls (greens). NASA scientists can track fall color by measuring how much red, orange, and yellow forests show compared with green. Tracking the ratio over time reveals where leaves are changing and when color peaks. The maps above show vegetation “redness” from September 29 to October 4 (left) and October 5 to 11 (right). Areas shown in green have values near 1, meaning the satellite detects about as much red as green, and most leaves have not yet turned. Areas shown in light yellow and red have higher values, indicating progressively more red pigment relative to green. The satellite detected particularly high levels of redness in parts of northern and eastern Russia, northern Alaska, and northern Canada from September 29 to October 4. In New England and upstate New York, redness began to fade during the week of October 5 to 11, even as it spread across much of the Midwest and the Mid-Atlantic. (Not all the yellows and reds on the maps represent fall colors. Crops in some agricultural areas, for instance, show high anthocyanin levels as they age and after they are harvested. Also, in some regions, clouds produce what appear to be gaps in the vegetation.) Seeing Red in Vermont Many of the reddest areas—such as the Adirondacks in New York, the Green Mountains in Vermont, and the White Mountains in New Hampshire—have large numbers of sugar maples (Acer saccharum) and red maples ( Acer rubrum) , deciduous trees that turn a brilliant shade of crimson in the fall. Blueberries, bilberries, sedges, mosses, and grasses likely contribute to the intense reds detected in marshy tundra areas in northern Alaska , Canada , and Russia . Red and orange hues cover the forested ridges of central Vermont, while river valleys and lower-elevation areas are still green. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on October 3, 2026. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured an image (above) of intensely red foliage around Ripton, Vermont, on October 3, 2026, around the peak of redness in the region. Poet Robert Frost, author of “ October ,” “ The Road Not Taken ,” “ Nothing Gold Can Stay ,” and several other poems that evoke fall foliage, kept a summer home and farm in Ripton and taught at Middlebury’s Bread Loaf School of English. Some other satellites with hyperspectral sensors can measure fall foliage pigments in a way that is similar to PACE, but only in more localized areas and less frequently. PACE is the first satellite capable of measuring all three key leaf pigments—anthocyanins, carotenoids, and chlorophylls—across the entire planet every day or two. “It’s the ability to collect time-series data of anthocyanins and carotenoids everywhere on Earth repeatedly that is game-changing,” said Karl Huemmrich , a vegetation scientist with the Goddard Earth Sciences Technology and Research II center at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. Huemmrich, who is also a member of the PACE science team, was eager to work with the satellite because of OCI’s broad swath and short revisit time. “The time-series data allow us to determine peak redness and yellowness anywhere on Earth,” he said. In the fall, leaves change colors as they lose chlorophyll, a green molecule that plants use to synthesize food. Since chlorophyll is not a stable compound, plants must continuously synthesize it, a process that requires ample sunlight and warm temperatures. As temperatures decrease and days shorten in autumn, levels of chlorophyll drop, causing greens to fade and presenting an opportunity for carotenoids and anthocyanins to show their colors. Observing Leaves in a Canopy Near You As part of the ongoing North American Phenology Campaign run by the Global Learning and Observations to Benefit the Environment ( GLOBE ) program, NASA data scientist Skye Caplan has been posting weekly foliage maps of vegetation redness. The maps show waves of red emerging in the high latitudes in August and shifting equatorward in September and October. The PACE team is asking the public to submit photos of fall foliage to help scientists “ground truth” the satellite observations and better understand how various factors influence vegetation color. Fall foliage sprinkles a forested New England landscape in a photo taken in Meredith, New Hampshire, on October 11, 2026, by a participant in GLOBE’s North America Phenology Campaign . GLOBE “Changes in pigments can also occur when vegetation is stressed due to drought or insect damage,” said Caplan. She noted that changes like these likely help explain why PACE measures high levels of redness in agricultural regions of Brazil, Australia, and Canada that don’t track closely with broader seasonal changes. “The more photos we can get from the ground, the better,” Caplan said. Ground photos help scientists refine PACE’s observations of vegetation color, which the team hopes will eventually support several lines of research. These include how the timing of spring greening and fall senescence is changing, how vegetation changes affect the global carbon cycle, and how leaf color influences wildfire risk. Scientists also want to know whether PACE can detect early warning signs of drought, insect infestations, and plant disease. People can participate in the GLOBE campaign even if they live in an area without dense forests or picturesque fall foliage displays. Scientists also want ground observations of shrubs, grasses, wildflowers, evergreens, crops, and other vegetation. But when it comes to “red leaf hunting,” don’t delay, Caplan said. “Color changes happen kind of slowly, then all at once, and then they’re gone.” NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using PACE data courtesy of Skye Caplan /NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . article.description: Where oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, belts of volcanoes known as continental arcs can form. Located around the world, these arcs may undergo episodic magma flare-ups—dramatic surges in the flow of magma into the continental crust at rates up to 20 times higher than normal. However, what triggers these extreme surges, which last tens of millions of years, can be unclear.

Sin embargo, lo que desencadena estos aumentos extremos, que duran decenas de millones de años, puede ser poco claro.

Sin embargo, lo que desencadena estos aumentos extremos, que duran decenas de millones de años, puede ser poco claro.

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Chipre: Isla de serpientes, gatos y ofiolitas.**

Chipre, una isla del Mediterráneo, ha sido objeto de estudio geológico y ecológico debido a su singular formación y biodiversidad. Según investigaciones, Chipre comenzó a formarse hace aproximadamente 90 millones de años durante el Cretácico tardío, cuando el magma del fondo marino solidificó y creó nueva corteza oceánica. Este proceso tectónico dio lugar a la aparición de ofiolitas, rocas que se asemejan a la piel de una serpiente, visibles en las montañas Troodos.

El Akrotiri Salt Lake, una laguna costera en la península de Akrotiri, ha sido un hábitat crucial para las aves migratorias, especialmente los flamencos. Sin embargo, la población de flamencos ha disminuido drásticamente, pasando de un promedio de 4,000 aves a solo 30 en 2025, lo que ha generado preocupación entre los ecologistas.

Además, la isla es conocida por su abundante población de gatos, que se estima iguala el número de habitantes, superando el millón. Esta situación se remonta a la antigüedad, cuando se importaron gatos desde Egipto para controlar la población de serpientes. Hoy, el Monasterio de San Nicolás de los Gatos sigue siendo un refugio para estos felinos, donde un grupo de monjas cuida de ellos.

NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous , with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building new oceanic crust . Over time, portions of this oceanic rock were wrenched upward by tectonic forces , eventually emerging as a rugged island made of ophiolite , a type of rock with a mottled green appearance said to look like the skin of a snake. Remnants of that ancient island are still visible in the dark rocks of the Troodos Mountains . During the Miocene , considerably younger layers of chalk, limestone, marl, and other marine sedimentary rocks accumulated around the island, providing material that developed into a second, smaller island to the south during a later period of geologic uplift . Over time, sediment poured from rivers into the channel separating the two islands and combined with marine sediments to create deltas and eventually two land bridges, or tombolos . The joined landmass comprises the Akrotiri Peninsula , now the southernmost tip of Cyprus. The sandy edges of the peninsula were visible when Landsat 8 captured these images on October 10, 2026. Akrotiri Salt Lake , a coastal lagoon that was once an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, lies between the two tombolos. The more westerly feature, the Kouris River tombolo, formed first, developing about 50,000 years ago from river-deposited gravels and sands. The eastern tombolo extended southward from Cyprus, cutting off the Mediterranean Sea only within the past 2,000 years, according to geologists . The lake’s water levels now vary markedly with the seasons, typically filling in the late autumn and winter and drying out in the summer. The influx of winter water has historically attracted sizable overwintering flamingo populations, averaging about 4,000 birds. However, the wintering flamingo population has declined in recent years, plummeting to 30 birds in 2025, according to news reports . Flamingos have long flocked to the lake to feed on fairy shrimp , which are rich in colorful substances called carotenoids that give the birds their famously pink hue . Snakes are another of the island’s more notorious animal inhabitants. In antiquity, Cyprus was known as Ophiousa , or “ land of snakes ,” likely due to its robust population of blunt-nosed vipers . According to legend, the island’s snake communities grew to be so problematic during a drought in the fourth century that the Roman Empress Helena , mother of Constantine the Great, called for shiploads of cats to be sent from Egypt to control the venomous reptiles. The first feline imports were released in a particularly snake-infested area on the southeastern part of the Akrotiri Peninsula, an area that came to be known as Cape Gata (Cape Cat in Greek). The cape today is still home to the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats , a place where legend says that monks encouraged newly arrived Egyptian cats to hunt snakes. Today, Cyprus has as many cats as people, with more than one million of the feline predators stalking the island. The handful of nuns who now live in the monastery still care for hundreds of cats, according to the St. Nicholas Center . A broader image of Cyprus captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 shows the western half of the island on October 10, 2026. article.description: NOAA, NASA release measurements of 2026 ozone hole While weather caused a greater loss of ozone this year, long-term recovery still on track November 4, 2026 NOAA Corps LT Michael Doneghey, the South Pole observatory station lead, holds a weather balloon while NOAA Station Technician Luke Longren carries a package containing an ozonesonde — an airborne instrument that measures ozone levels — just prior to launch on October 18, 2026. (Image credit: Tommy Jensen/Amentum. With permission.) Atypical weather conditions caused the Antarctic ozone hole to grow to an unusually large size in 2026, NOAA and NASA scientists reported today, though they said the protective ozone layer is still on track to recover by later this century. Fueled by a powerful polar vortex, the 2026 ozone hole became the seventh-largest in 48 years of monitoring, based on NOAA and NASA analysis of the seasonal mean area. However, scientists noted that this year’s hole would have been larger still if levels of ozone-destroying chemicals in the atmosphere had not been reduced through international cooperation. During peak ozone depletion season between September 7 and October 13, 2026, the average extent of the hole covered about 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers) — more than twice the area of the United States. Scientists continually track the amount of ozone in the stratosphere because it acts as Earth’s “sunscreen,” helping shield life from harmful solar radiation. This is distinct from ground level ozone, which is an air pollutant commonly resulting from human activities. “The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.” The hole reached its greatest extent for the year on September 18 at 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That’s about 90% as large as the largest ozone hole ever observed, which occurred on September 9, 2000. “The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” Newman said. How does ozone loss occur? The ozone depletion process begins when human-made compounds containing chlorine and bromine are released into the environment. Air currents carry the gases up into the stratosphere, where they’re broken down by ultraviolet radiation. The freed chlorine and bromine atoms interact with cloud particles in the Antarctic stratosphere to enable ozone destruction. The stratospheric polar vortex , a seasonal stream of wind encircling Antarctica, plays a key role by corralling the frigid air necessary to produce polar stratospheric clouds. “The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. “That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.” How do scientists measure and monitor the ozone hole? The depletion of ozone within the hole was not as severe as record-breaking holes that occurred 10 or 20 years ago. Deploying balloon-borne instruments from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory , and using an optical instrument called the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer , NOAA scientists found that ozone concentrations directly overhead reached their lowest value for the year — 105 Dobson units — on October 17. The Dobson unit is the commonly used standard of measurement for expressing ozone concentration. One hundred Dobson Units represents a column of ozone that would be 1 millimeter deep – about as thick as a dime – if compressed under standard temperature and pressure conditions at sea level. The lowest value ever recorded over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006. Since 1979, satellites have also been integral to monitoring the health of the ozone layer. Instruments aboard NASA’s Aura satellite, the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, jointly operated by NASA and NOAA, all contributed to the annual monitoring. NOAA and NASA scientists said that the ongoing monitoring shows that controls established by the Montreal Protocol in 1987 continue to drive long-term recovery of stratospheric ozone. As part of the Montreal Protocol, the international community committed to replacing ozone-depleting substances like chlorofluorocarbons with less-harmful alternatives. Since their peak, chlorine levels in the Antarctic stratosphere derived from ozone-depleting substances have declined by about a third relative to levels reached in the 1980s, said Stephen Montzka, senior scientist at NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory. What chemicals can cause the loss of ozone? Chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once widely used in consumer goods such as refrigerators, air conditioners, and building insulation. They can linger in the atmosphere or leach out of old products and landfills for many decades. As those older compounds break down, scientists estimate that the ozone hole will recover by the 2070s. More: View the latest status of the ozone layer over the Antarctic by visiting NOAA’s South Pole Ozone website and NASA’s Ozone Watch . article.source_body: For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov . Download PDF here Chip resistors are widely used in NASA projects, yet cases of alumina substrate cracking during environmental testing are rare. Two instances of thick-film chip resistor cracking were observed during thermal cycling after vibration, with fractures occurring across the short axis due to bending. Failure analyses ruled out defective lots and fatigue, identifying board flexure, component orientation, excessive solder, and mounting stresses as contributing factors. The bulletin recommends careful component placement, finite element analysis, controlled solder fillet height, thorough inspection, and functional thermal shock testing to mitigate flexure-induced cracking risks in ceramic body components on printed circuit boards. Background The NESC noted historical lack of reported cases of chip resistors’ alumina substrate cracking during vibration and thermal cycling, although chip resistors are ubiquitous across NASA projects. Two instances of thick film chip resistor body cracking were observed during environmental acceptance testing on printed circuit board assemblies. Both failures occurred during thermal cycling after vibration testing, exhibiting intermittent open circuit failures at hot dwell temperatures that recovered at room temperature. Transverse fracture occurred at the mid-span of each resistor, running parallel to the terminations. The two resistors were installed in similar locations near the edge of the boards on two identical boards. Cracks in failed resistors were along the short axis of the resistor due to apparent bending of the resistors, Figure 1. Resistors showed no signs of pre-existing defects. Causal Relationships Initial theories pointed to vibration-induced damage of potentially defective resistors since both resistors came from the same production lot. However, the resistor lot not only meets the requirements of procurement specification MIL-PRF-55342 but additional tests were performed and did not reveal any direct evidence of a defective resistor lot. There was no evidence of an elevated risk of defective resistors within the production lot. Failure Analyses Independent failure analyses concluded that the cracked chip resistors were due to bending/tensile failures. There was no clear-cut root cause or visible defect identifying a crack initiation site. Both resistors exhibited a single, straight crack across the short axis (perpendicular to the long axis), indicating a bending/tensile failure without twisting. The damage signatures are not consistent with cyclic fatigue, likely ruling out fatigue failure during vibration. In addition, NESC independent optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Figure 2, of both resistors did not identify any clear flaw locations for fatigue damage initiation and progression; therefore, the possibility of defective resistors as well as fatigue vibration as the root cause becomes unlikely. Cause Conclusions No direct root cause was identified, but contributing factors leading to increased design consideration needed for large footprint ceramic components located near the edges of a printed circuit board that can lead to stress cracks due to manufacturing or installation bow/twist of the printed circuit board include: Location of the relatively large resistors (case size 2512) next to the edge of the board with resistor’s long axis parallel to the card edge, increasing susceptibility to board flexure-induced damage. Excessive solder that extended to the top pads on the resistor terminations. Excessive bending moments or loads resulting from board bow/twist. Hard mounting the board to a rigid frame, which can store and amplify these bow/twist stresses. Suboptimal fastener torquing patterns, which may concentrate mounting stresses specifically at the resistor locations. Guidelines for Assembly of Ceramic Body Components to Printed Circuit Boards The following guidelines are to be considered given the recent experience. Component Orientation: Avoid orienting the long axis of large footprint ceramic components parallel to nearby printed circuit board edges to reduce susceptibility to global and local flexure damage. Finite Element Analysis: Perform sufficient Finite Element Analysis to demonstrate adequate stress and displacement margins on large components when they must be placed near the edge of the board. Solder Joint Fillet Limits: Keep solder off the top surface of terminations. Solder on top creates a rigid joint that transfers printed circuit board flexure directly into the ceramic increasing risk of flexure-induced cracking. Consult the individual parts manufacturers for guidance, as they may place specific limits on solder fillet height. Solder Joint Inspection: Inspect physical solder joints or review photographic images of the joints to verify that components have sufficient, but not excessive, solder fillets according to manufacturer limits. Functional Thermal Shock Testing: Perform one to three thermal cycles, including a hot-dwell functional test, prior to vibration testing, to document as built component integrity. References 1. **TITULAR: El Desafío Universitario de la NASA Enciende la Trayectoria de un Emprendedor de Drones**

Gavin Gardner, un joven emprendedor de Michigan, ha transformado su experiencia en el Desafío Universitario de la NASA en una exitosa carrera en el desarrollo de drones. En 2024, junto a su hermano Gryson y otros exalumnos del programa, fundó AG3 Labs, una empresa dedicada a la fabricación de drones para ejercicios de entrenamiento militar.

Gardner, quien fue estudiante de ingeniería en la Universidad Estatal de Michigan, participó en el programa de la NASA que otorga subvenciones a equipos de estudiantes universitarios. Su primer proyecto, Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), buscaba innovar en la entrega de carga mediante drones que se acoplaran a autobuses urbanos. Aunque el equipo decidió no comercializar esta idea debido a las estrictas regulaciones, su trabajo les valió un segundo premio en 2023 para desarrollar el sistema Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS).

La experiencia adquirida en el Desafío Universitario no solo les proporcionó habilidades técnicas, sino también conocimientos en gestión empresarial, lo que ha sido crucial para el crecimiento de AG3 Labs. Actualmente, la compañía produce miles de drones al mes, consolidándose como un actor importante en el sector de la tecnología de defensa.

article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Four co-founders of AG3 Labs –from left Matt Atkinson, Gavin Gardner, Ryan Atkinson, and Gryson Gardner – show off the military training drones their company builds at a U.S. Army event at Camp Grayling in Michigan. As a student, Gavin was on a Michigan State team twice selected for participation in NASA’s University Student Research Challenge. His NASA experience served as a foundation for the creation of AG3. AG3 Labs Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge. Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students in a lab setting, he and his team were completely new to things like creating budgets, handling large sums of money, and promoting their work for crowdfunding. That’s why demonstrating both engineering and entrepreneurship skills are major tentpoles of NASA’s University Student Research Challenge (USRC), an initiative that provides grants to teams of college students interested in helping the agency realize its aeronautical research goals. “Half the battle is building your product,” Gardner said recently. “The other half is selling the product in a way that everyone else can understand what you’re doing and not talking in nerdy, engineering ways.” We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers. STEVEN HOLZ NASA USRC Manager Gardner and his Michigan State USRC alumni teammates are still using those lessons today, as aerospace developers. In 2024, they founded their own company, AG3 Labs, which specializes in drones for military training exercises. “I don’t think I would discredit our technical expertise in getting us to where we are today, but I know that USRC was a booster that really amplified our trajectory at such a young age,” Gardner said. NASA USRC manager Steven Holz said Gardner’s experience shows what students can accomplish when they receive both a grant and guidance – enabling a future workforce and contributing to the aviation industry. “We are proud to see the success of USRC alumni,” Holz said. “We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.” Research path Gardner’s path to running his own company began with a middle school age trip to Space Camp, where he began realizing that he wanted to be an engineer. The engineering bug also bit his brother, Gryson Gardner, and the two of them would often be found in their Michigan garage tinkering with various machinery, including drones and electronic kits. When Gardner arrived at Michigan State, he looked for extracurricular groups and found one dedicated to the increasingly popular hobby of drones. He gained hands-on, practical experience in how drones are made and operated. In 2021, Gardner received an email from a friend who told him they had just won a USRC grant from NASA for an activity called Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), and they needed help building a new drone. “We had this idea that instead of flying through the whole city, why can’t a drone just hitchhike a ride on a city bus like everyone else does?” Gardner said. The concept was for a cargo-carrying drone to take off, dock on top of public transportation such as a bus, charge its batteries while riding along, and then take off for its final leg of the delivery. The team built and flew a full-scale drone to prove the concept but decided against pursuing a commercial venture. “The commercial drone market kind of scared us a little bit with the large number of regulations that go into operating such a novel idea like this with flying over people in a dense city,” Gardner said. But the team’s demonstration of technical prowess and confidence led to a second USRC award from NASA in 2023 – the Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS), which focused on using a laser to transfer power directly to a drone in flight. While working on LEADS, which led to flying a prototype, Gardner’s network of contacts within the drone community expanded to include NASA personnel at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, who made him aware of internship opportunities, which he applied for and was accepted while in graduate school. Gavin Gardner, a University Student Research Challenge participant who went on to co-found his own drone company, also was a NASA intern in 2024 and wrote this social media post. Student challenge paves way for opportunity As his graduation in the spring of 2025 with a master’s degree approached, Gardner took the initial steps in late 2024 to co-found with his brother and other USRC alumni AG3 Labs after a friend suggested the military could use low-cost drones to test effective counter drone systems. An initial award from the U.S. Army led to more contracts, allowing the company to expand and ramp up its operations, where today their production capability enables thousands of drones to be built each month. Gardner credits his experience with USRC, especially when it came to learning more about the business side of running a technical operation, with helping create the opportunities for success he and his team are experiencing today. **TITULAR: Colores de la Luna: Un fenómeno astronómico documentado en Chile**

El 1 de noviembre de 2026, la comunidad astronómica chilena se vio sorprendida por la variedad de colores que presentó la Luna en el cielo nocturno. Este fenómeno, que ha sido objeto de estudio por parte de astrofotógrafos, se debe a la interacción de la luz lunar con la atmósfera terrestre, la cual puede alterar la percepción del color del satélite natural.

En Chile, donde la observación astronómica es favorecida por su cielo despejado, se han registrado diferentes tonalidades de la Luna, desde un intenso rojo hasta un azul más raro. Estos colores son el resultado de la dispersión de la luz, especialmente cuando la Luna se encuentra cerca del horizonte, donde la atmósfera terrestre actúa como un filtro, eliminando ciertas longitudes de onda de luz.

Astrofotógrafos locales han documentado estos cambios a lo largo de los años, contribuyendo a la comprensión de cómo factores como la presencia de polvo en la atmósfera pueden influir en la apariencia lunar. Este fenómeno no solo enriquece la experiencia visual de los observadores, sino que también abre nuevas líneas de investigación en meteorología y astronomía. La fascinación por estos colores invita a más chilenos a mirar hacia el cielo y explorar los misterios del universo.

Colors of the Moon Explanation: What color is the Moon? It depends on the night — and the time. Outside of the Earth’s atmosphere , the dark Moon , which shines by reflected sunlight, appears a magnificent ly brown-tinged gray. The featured image highlights a collection of apparent colors of the full moon on Earth, documented by one astrophotographer over 10 years from different locations across Italy . A red – or yellow -colored moon usually indicates a moon seen near the horizon . There, some of the blue light has been scattered away by a long path through the Earth’s atmosphere , sometimes laden with fine dust. A blue-colored moon is more rare and can indicate an atmosphere carrying larger dust particles . What created the purple moon is unclear — it may be a combination of several effects. The last image captures the total lunar eclipse of 2018 July — where the moon, in Earth’s shadow , appeared a faint red — due to light refracted through air around the Earth. **TITULAR: NASA selecciona 19 nuevas propuestas de ciencia ciudadana en 2026**

En un avance significativo para la ciencia colaborativa, la NASA ha seleccionado 19 nuevas propuestas de ciencia ciudadana en 2026, reafirmando su compromiso con la investigación accesible y participativa. Este anuncio se enmarca dentro del programa de financiamiento de semillas para la ciencia ciudadana, que busca involucrar a voluntarios en proyectos científicos innovadores.

Entre los proyectos destacados se encuentra "The Rogue Worlds Project", liderado por Jacqueline Faherty del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, que invita a los participantes a buscar planetas libres en datos de la misión SPHEREx. Otro proyecto, "Planet Hunters Roman", dirigido por Bernard Gaudi de la Universidad Estatal de Ohio, se centra en la detección de exoplanetas a través de la lente de la nueva telescopía espacial Nancy Grace Roman.

Además, el programa incluye iniciativas en heliophysics y ciencias planetarias, como "Space Weather UnderGround", que permitirá a los ciudadanos monitorear la magnetosfera terrestre mediante magnetómetros. Estas propuestas no solo amplían el alcance de la investigación científica, sino que también fomentan la participación activa de la comunidad en la exploración del cosmos.
