article.source_body: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science NASA Selects 19 New Citizen… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project announced that their project volunteers have now discovered most of the known brown dwarfs , celestial objects that are similar to planets. The Zooniverse platform, with grant from NASA, reached a milestone of 1 billion classifications. Several projects have come online that leverage new super intelligence (SI) techniques to amplify or extend the work of volunteers. More NASA volunteers are using SI to build their own data tools and help write scientific papers than ever before. Even with all of those achievements, our science community is already working on the next round of new volunteer projects and innovations. NASA’s Science Mission Directorate has selected nineteen proposals from research teams in 2026 that will result in new opportunities for you to do NASA science. The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program (CSSFP-25) of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate aims to support scientists and other experts to develop citizen science projects and expand the pool of professional scientists who use citizen science techniques in their science investigations. Twelve new proposals to this program were selected. Astrophysics “The Rogue Worlds Project: Activating volunteers to uncover the hidden population of super Jupiters with SPHEREx” led by Principal Investigator Jacqueline Faherty from the American Museum of Natural History. This project will invite you to search data from NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission to find free-floating planets and brown dwarfs in clusters of young stars. The SPHEREx space observatory mapping the entire sky in near-infrared wavelengths. “ Quantifying the calibrations between intrinsic galaxy merger timescales with visual pair/tidal-feature classifications” led by Principal Investigator Kameswara Bharadwaj Mantha of the University of Missouri. This project will investigate galaxy mergers, helping astronomers understand how galaxies evolve through time. You will be invited to classify realistic mock images of galaxies to help probe the statistics and dynamical evolution of galaxy mergers. “ Overlap Zoo; cosmic light tables for galaxy transparency” led by Principal Investigator Benne Holwerda of the University of Louisville. Galaxies, which glow with the light of the billions of stars they contain, also contain dust. This dust is easiest to see and quantify when it overlaps, or is backlit by, another galaxy. Help spot and characterize these rare overlapping galaxy pairs to help reveal how much dust they contain. Overlap Zoo is live! Follow this link to learn more and join the project. “ Planet Hunters Roman: Extending Citizen Science to Planetary Microlensing” led by Principal Investigator Bernard Gaudi of the Ohio State University. Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars other than our Sun. Their gravity can bend the light that travels around them. This project will invite you to spot exoplanets in data from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope data by the way they bend starlight. Heliophysics “Space Weather UnderGround: Deploying a low-cost Magnetometer Array with Citizens for Heliophysics Research” led by Principal Investigator Hyunju Connor at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. Along with sunshine, our Sun produces the solar wind, an unrelenting flow of charged particles. Earth’s protective magnetic field shield deflects most of these particles, but not all, and not during extreme events. Help scientists monitor the subtle disturbances of Earth’s magnetosphere by the solar wind by setting up and monitoring your own magnetometer in Alaska. “A Citizen Science Initiative for Sonified Plasma Wave Characterization” led by Principal Investigator Lauren Blum of the University Of Colorado, Boulder. “Plasma” is the name given to the ionized gases at the edge of Earth’s magnetosphere. Solar wind, the rain of charged particles that flows out from the Sun, can interact with and generate waves in the plasma. This project will turn data from this dynamic zone into sound signals. You will be invited to listen in to identify waves in the Earth’s magnetosphere. “Revealing the Consequences of Foreshock Transients for Earth’s Magnetospheric System Through Participatory Science” led by Principal Investigator Wenli Mo at the Johns Hopkins University. This project will invite you to examine data from NASA’s MMS (Magnetospheric Multiscale) mission to identify “foreshock transients,” phenomena that have a critical but poorly understood role in space weather. The resulting dataset will help reveal how foreshock transients form, their properties, and their impacts. “IMPACT: Interactive Magnetospheric Particle Analysis and Citizen Technology” led by Principal Investigator Muhammad Fraz Bashir at the University of California, Los Angeles. Energetic particles rain down from the magnetosphere into the upper ionosphere, heating and perturbing the ionosphere, disrupting the scatter of radio waves and GPS operations. This project will invite you to help match patterns between two types of data: measurements from satellites flying overhead that detect energetic particles raining down from space and measurements from ground-based instruments that detect electromagnetic waves. By comparing these patterns, volunteers will help scientists figure out which types of space waves are causing different kinds of particle precipitation, and in turn, help scientists better understand and predict disruptions to GPS and increased radiation risks during space weather events. “Unlocking Clues About Particle Acceleration and Transport Using Particle Distributions” led by Principal Investigator Gang Kai Poh at the Catholic University Of America. NASA’s Advanced Composition Explorer, Parker Solar Probe, and Solar Orbiter are complementary missions gathering data to help scientists improve understanding of the Sun, solar wind, and space weather. Examine data from these missions to contribute to the study of the complicated flow of energetic particles from the Sun. “Data Fusion in Space: Combining Citizen Observations to Classify Solar Wind Tracers” led by Principal Investigator Cynthia Lopez-Portela of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. This project will invite you to use their pattern-recognition skills to spot features in images of the Sun’s corona, where the solar wind begins. These features can be used as tracers to help scientists track the movement of the solar wind and build better models of how it behaves. Planetary Sciences “Mapping Lunar Iron Abundance Hotspots to Enable In-Situ Resource Utilization of Regolith Consolidation Technologies” led by Principal Investigator Karen Martirosyan at the University of Texas, Rio Grande Valley. Building a base on the Moon will require creative use of Moon materials. So what materials will future teams of astronaut base-builders have to work with? This project will invite you to help locate iron deposits in data from NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper mission to help understand how the Moon formed and to aid future exploration. “Small Body Discovery and Outburst Monitoring with a Worldwide Citizen Science Telescope Network” led by Principal Investigator Ariel Graykowski at the SETI Institute. This project proposes to activate a global network of citizen scientists, each equipped with a standardized small-aperture telescope, to conduct follow-up observation of cometary outbursts and small moving bodies (comets, near-Earth asteroids, and main-belt asteroids). With their global distribution and a program of twilight observations, amateurs will complement professional surveys. The project will develop systems to automate processing of contributed images and to distribute alerts for objects of interest to the network. The Science Activation Program The Science Activation Program (SciAct) from NASA’s Science Mission Directorate supports a portfolio of competitively selected, collaborative project teams that extend the impact of NASA science. These “SciAct Teams” accomplish this by connecting people and communities – many of whom would not otherwise meaningfully engage – with NASA science data and experts, local partnerships, and authentic science experiences. Seven teams selected in the latest round of competition will engage learners with citizen science efforts directly related to NASA research priorities. Several other selected teams plan to incorporate citizen science projects or community science projects (research efforts led by and focused on specific communities) into their work. The selected proposals include: “Growing Beyond Earth: Science Activation Through Distributed Space Crop Research” led by Principal Investigator Carl Lewis at Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden, Inc. To travel or live in space, humans will need to eat. Growing Beyond Earth trains and equips middle- and high-school classrooms to conduct growth experiments with seeds and crops being evaluated for use as space food. “Sungrazer 2.0: From Armchair Discovery to Data-Driven Comet Science” led by Principal Investigator MaryKay Severino of the ARISA Lab and science lead Karl Battams of the Naval Research Laboratory. The original Sungrazer Project launched in 2006 in response to requests from citizen scientists for verification of comet discoveries. Since then, project volunteers have identified 5,204 comets and counting – the majority of known comets. Sungrazer 2.0 will bring the thrill of comet discovery to new audiences who will join the hunt for comets in images from NASA’s SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) and STEREO (Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory) missions. “Discovering the SPARC: Space Physics through Amateur Radio Communications” led by Principal Investigator Nathaniel Frissell of the University of Scranton. Since 2017 amateur radio operators have worked together in the Ham Radio Science Citizen Investigation (HamSCI) community to study Earth’s ionosphere through carefully designed and conducted investigations of how their signals bounce off this high, ionized layer of Earth’s atmosphere. This project will bring hands-on space weather science to communities nationwide through amateur radio equipment and enroll high schools in a national research network. “Telescopes for All: Promoting audience engagement with NASA science via participatory data experiences using robotic telescopes” led by Principal Investigator Mary Dussault of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. This project will expand public access to a suite of 22 user-friendly, professional robotic telescopes. This access will allow people to observe, analyze, and contribute to NASA-aligned research, including the search and study of exoplanets and other citizen science projects. “Researchers Inspiring Public Participation in Lake Education and Science (RIPPLES)” led by Principal Investigator Sarah Yelton and science lead Tamlin Pavelsky, both at the University Of North Carolina, Chapel Hill. This project will collaborate with the Lake Observations by Citizen Scientists and Satellites (LOCSS) project to expand participation in lake and reservoir level monitoring. Submitted data will be used to validate observations such as those made by NASA’s SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography) mission. “ARK (Antarctic Resilience and Knowledge): A Collaborative Network for Discovery and Education of Antarctica’s Iconic Species and their Changing Habitats” led by Principal Investigator Sharon Stammerjohn at the University of Colorado, Boulder. This project will invite you to examine NASA’s very high-resolution satellite images of Antarctica to study and monitor habitat changes affecting penguin, seal, and whale populations. With validation by scientists and integration of machine-assisted detection tools, this project will expand the analytical capacity of Antarctic researchers and build public literacy in polar ecosystem science. “Arctic Learning and Engagement with NASA Data for Community Solutions (Arctic LENS)” led by Principal Investigator Katie Spellman of the University of Alaska Fairbanks. This project will invite Alaskans to contribute seasonal environmental monitoring (snow, ice, aurora, spring ice-out, and green-up) in support of NASA missions including FORTE (Arctic Coastlines: Frontlines of Rapidly Transforming Ecosystems), SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography), PACE (Phytoplankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem), and Landsat. Explore citizen science awards from previous years: November 2025 January 2024 September 2023 August 2022 July 2021 For more information on NASA’s citizen science programs, visit https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science . **TITULAR: La galaxia no tan oculta, IC 342, revela secretos sobre su formación**

**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

La galaxia IC 342, también conocida como Caldwell 5, ha sido objeto de un nuevo estudio que arroja luz sobre su historia y características. Ubicada a aproximadamente 10 millones de años luz de la Tierra, IC 342 es uno de los miembros más brillantes del grupo IC 342/Maffei, que se encuentra relativamente cerca del Grupo Local, donde reside nuestra propia Vía Láctea.

Investigaciones recientes han permitido observar esta galaxia a través del denso plano de la Vía Láctea, que está lleno de gas, polvo y estrellas. Este enfoque ha corregido malentendidos previos sobre la historia de IC 342, que incluían la teoría de que había sido eyectada del Grupo Local. Los nuevos datos sugieren que la galaxia tiene su propio polvo que interfiere con la luz del hidrógeno, lo que indica la presencia de estrellas jóvenes y brillantes.

Además, los mapas de campos magnéticos de IC 342 han proporcionado pistas sobre uno de los grandes enigmas galácticos: la formación de los brazos espirales. Estos hallazgos no solo enriquecen nuestro conocimiento sobre IC 342, sino que también ofrecen nuevas perspectivas sobre la dinámica de las galaxias en el universo.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 4 – The… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. The Not-So-Hidden Galaxy, IC 342 Explanation: “I see” IC 342, the Hidden Galaxy! Today’s image peers through the plane of the Milky Way , through all its gas, dust and stars, to unveil this spiral galaxy . IC 342 (or Caldwell 5 ) is one of the brightest members of the IC 342/ Maffei group of galaxies. Located about 10 million light years away, this group is quite close to the Local Group that includes our Milky Way. Inaccurate accounting of the crowded and dusty Milky Way foreground has led to misunderstandings in IC 342’s history, including the theory that the galaxy was ejected from the Local Group . IC 342 has its own dust intermittently blocking the glow of hydrogen gas , indicating the presence of bright, young stars. Magnetic field maps of IC 342 reveal that magnetic fields may contribute substantially to one of the biggest galactic puzzles: how do spiral arms form ? **TITULAR: Caltech nombra al comandante de Artemis II, Reid Wiseman, como subdirector de NASA JPL**

Reid Wiseman, el comandante de la misión Artemis II, ha sido nombrado como el nuevo subdirector del Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) de la NASA y vicepresidente asociado de Caltech. Su incorporación a estas instituciones de prestigio comenzará el 30 de noviembre de 2026. Wiseman, un astronauta emérito y capitán retirado de la Marina de los EE. UU., ha tenido una carrera destacada en la exploración espacial, incluyendo un histórico vuelo lunar que lo llevó a recorrer 695,081 millas, la mayor distancia jamás alcanzada por humanos.

El administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, destacó la experiencia y el liderazgo de Wiseman, afirmando que su trayectoria en misiones de alta complejidad lo convierte en un activo valioso para el JPL. Durante su tiempo en la NASA, Wiseman ha liderado la seguridad de vuelos tripulados y ha participado en numerosas investigaciones científicas.

En su nuevo rol, será responsable de la dirección estratégica y la mejora continua de las operaciones del laboratorio, además de actuar como el principal enlace para programas de seguridad nacional. Este nombramiento se produce en un momento crucial, ya que el JPL se prepara para celebrar su 90 aniversario, consolidando su legado en la exploración espacial.

article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Former NASA astronaut and Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman joins Caltech and NASA JPL as Caltech associate vice president and JPL deputy director on Nov. 30. Photo Credit: NASA Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on Nov. 30, 2026. “Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “As commander of Artemis II, he helped carry America back around the Moon, and now, as an emeritus astronaut, he will continue giving back to NASA from a new vantage point at JPL. Reid is joining a storied laboratory that has made an enormous amount of history, and there is a lot more ahead. I am excited to see what he and the JPL team accomplish in the years to come.” During the Artemis II test flight, Wiseman , Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen journeyed 695,081 miles on a lunar flyby that took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before. “It feels fitting for Reid, who with the Artemis II crew traveled farther from Earth than any human in history, to join Caltech and JPL — institutions that for nearly 90 years have sent spacecraft into the far reaches of our solar system and beyond,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director and Caltech vice president. “Reid shares our drive for discovery, knows what it takes to lead teams through high-stakes missions, and has a remarkable ability to inspire people everywhere. He adds incredible bench strength to our leadership team as we build on the lab’s legacy and shape its future together.” After joining NASA’s astronaut corps in 2009, Wiseman went on to serve as flight engineer aboard the International Space Station for the 165-day Expedition 41 mission in 2014 and was a commander of NASA’s 21st Extreme Environment Mission Operations expedition, during which he lived for eight days in a habitat on the ocean floor in 2016. As the agency’s chief astronaut from December 2020 to November 2022, Wiseman led NASA’s astronaut corps, overseeing crew flight readiness and crew safety for all NASA human spaceflight missions. During his years of service at the agency, he has conducted hundreds of scientific experiments. “I’ve explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the Sun disappear behind the Moon from deep space. But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation,” Wiseman said. “What an awesome time in my career to join this team and to try and push humanity and push our understanding of the solar system and the universe.” Wiseman joins JPL, NASA’s only federally funded research and development center, as the lab approaches its 90th anniversary since being founded by Caltech. In his role as Caltech’s associate vice president and JPL deputy director, Wiseman will be responsible for the strategic leadership, stewardship and continuous improvement of laboratory operations, including close partnership with Caltech on institutional planning, management and compliance. Serving as Center Management Authority for JPL mission execution, Wiseman will ensure operational excellence across mission support functions in accordance with NASA requirements and applicable federal and state regulations. In addition, he will be JPL’s primary interface for national security programs. “Reid brings to Caltech and JPL a truly unprecedented view of what humanity can achieve when ingenuity and determination are matched with the courage to pursue the furthest frontiers,” said Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana. “His pioneering spirit coupled with unbounded curiosity make him a natural fit for Caltech and JPL, a force-multiplier for a community whose daring continues to push the limits of humanity’s reach. I look forward to working closely with Dave and Reid as we chart our next era of exploration in partnership with NASA, elevating America’s space ambitions to breathtaking new heights.” After receiving a bachelor’s degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Wiseman joined the Navy, going on to fly combat missions and serve as a test pilot. **APOD: 6 de noviembre de 2026 – Un adiós a Swift**

El 4 de noviembre de 2026, el observatorio Neil Gehrels Swift de la NASA reingresó a la atmósfera terrestre, marcando el fin de una misión que duró casi 22 años. Este satélite, que se destacó por su capacidad de observar explosiones cósmicas de gran energía, dejó un legado invaluable en el estudio del universo.

Swift contaba con una combinación de instrumentos, incluyendo telescopios de rayos X y gamma, que permitieron a los científicos investigar fenómenos como las explosiones de rayos gamma con un nivel de detalle sin precedentes. La reciente actividad solar, que incluyó un máximo solar, aceleró la degradación de su órbita, lo que llevó a la decisión de intentar una misión de rescate que, lamentablemente, no tuvo éxito.

A pesar de su desaparición, los datos recopilados por Swift seguirán iluminando el camino para futuras investigaciones. Su legado no solo reside en los descubrimientos realizados, sino también en la inspiración que brinda para nuevas misiones espaciales. La comunidad científica espera que estos avances continúen impulsando la exploración del cosmos.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 6 – A… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Farewell to Swift Explanation: It is time to say goodbye to NASA ‘s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory . After nearly 22 years of service, the satellite re-entered Earth’s atmosphere on November 4 at 7:39 EST over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia . The featured image is a mosaic created in 2018 using the first one million images captured by the satellite’s Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope . Swift had a combination of instruments, including an X-ray telescope and a gamma-ray telescope , that worked together to enable humanity to study, in unprecedented detail, the fastest and most energetic explosions in the universe. The most recent solar maximum accelerated the decay of the satellite’s orbit. An innovative mission to rescue Swift by boosting its orbit was not successful . Swift burned on reentry like a shooting star, but the impressive data acquired by the telescope over its mission will continue to bring light to the mysteries of the cosmos for years to come. May it keep inspiring new missions to boldly go into space, explore new data and seek out new science. Tomorrow’s picture: what’s next? El satélite Swift de NASA reingresó a la atmósfera tras 22 años de importantes descubrimientos astronómicos.

El 4 de noviembre de 2026, el observatorio Neil Gehrels Swift de la NASA reingresó a la atmósfera terrestre, marcando el fin de una misión que duró casi 22 años. Este satélite, que se destacó por su capacidad de observar explosiones cósmicas de gran energía, dejó un legado invaluable en el estudio del universo. Swift contaba con una combinación de instrumentos, incluyendo telescopios de rayos X y gamma, que permitieron a los científicos investigar fenómenos como las explosiones de rayos gamma con un nivel de detalle sin precedentes. La reciente actividad solar, que incluyó un máximo solar, aceleró la degradación de su órbita, lo que llevó a la decisión de intentar una misión de rescate que, lamentablemente, no tuvo éxito. A pesar de su desaparición, los datos recopilados por Swift seguirán iluminando el camino para futuras investigaciones. Su legado no solo reside en los descubrimientos realizados, sino también en la inspiración que brinda para nuevas misiones espaciales. La comunidad científica espera que estos avances continúen impulsando la exploración del cosmos.

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Webb revela un impresionante panorama de formación estelar**

El telescopio James Webb ha proporcionado una imagen asombrosa de la región de formación estelar IC 348, ubicada a solo 1000 años luz en la constelación de Perseo. Esta imagen es una de las más grandes liberadas hasta ahora y ha permitido a los astrónomos investigar la presencia de enanas marrones, objetos menos masivos que las estrellas más pequeñas.

Recientemente, los investigadores han descubierto enanas marrones con masas tan bajas como el doble de la de Júpiter, lo que representa un nuevo rango en el estudio de estos cuerpos celestes. Estas enanas marrones se forman de manera similar a las estrellas, pero sus núcleos nunca alcanzan temperaturas suficientes para fusionar hidrógeno en helio. Este hallazgo desafía los modelos actuales sobre la formación estelar.

Además, uno de los nuevos objetos descubiertos muestra signos de un disco, lo que sugiere que podrían estar formándose planetas a su alrededor. También se identificó una característica en los espectros de estas enanas que indica la presencia de hidrocarburos, lo que sugiere que estos objetos podrían pertenecer a una clase espectral única.

La investigación en IC 348 continúa, con el objetivo de entender mejor la diversidad de objetos de masa planetaria en diferentes regiones de formación estelar.

article.description: La vista de un rostro helado parecido a un cráneo en la isla antártica podría hacer que la sangre se te helara.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Isla Vega Congelada en Terror**

En un inquietante hallazgo, imágenes satelitales de la isla Vega, ubicada en el mar de Weddell, han revelado que parte de su superficie helada presenta la apariencia de un cráneo sonriente. Este fenómeno, observado por primera vez en marzo de 2025 y nuevamente en octubre de 2026, ha sido documentado por el Earth Observatory de la NASA. La transformación de la isla se debe a la exposición de hielo desnudo, resultado de temperaturas inusualmente altas durante el invierno de 2026.

El glaciólogo Mauri Pelto, de Nichols College, señala que la falta de acumulación de nieve y el efecto de la sublimación han contribuido a la disminución de la masa de hielo en la isla. Las imágenes muestran un contraste notable entre la capa de nieve en marzo y la ausencia de esta en octubre, lo que sugiere un acelerado proceso de derretimiento. Este fenómeno no solo afecta la morfología de la isla, sino que también plantea preocupaciones sobre el futuro de los glaciares en la región.

La isla Vega tiene una historia trágica, siendo parte de la expedición antártica sueca de 1901-1903, donde los exploradores enfrentaron condiciones extremas. Hoy, el cambio climático amenaza con alterar aún más este paisaje helado, lo que podría tener repercusiones significativas en el ecosistema antártico.

NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin March 22, 2025 October 10, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island. These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) A nunatak jutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, a lateral moraine forms a mouth, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible. Above-average temperatures in winter 2026 —particularly in June —were partly responsible for so much bare ice in October , said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.” The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Bare ice is darker than snow and absorbs more solar energy, meaning that melting is poised to speed up as the days grow longer and warmer. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.” October 10, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin The first comprehensive mapping of Vega Island’s ice was aided by Landsat imagery. In a study published in 1982 , scientists described the island’s four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers. They leveraged early Landsat observations along with aerial photos and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers on Vega. Of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier has been closely monitored since the austral summer of 1998-1999, with researchers measuring an overall decline in its mass. Satellite images acquired in recent decades show ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock. Long before scientists began tracking its glaciers, Vega was a bright spot in a tale of terror born out of early exploration of the area. The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife on and around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party became split into three groups during their explorations, isolated for a winter in different locations. Adding to the horror, they lost their ship to the pack ice. Cape Well-met, as it would come to be known, off the “forehead” of the Vega Island skull, was the site of a happy reunion of two of the groups in spring 1903. Soon thereafter, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors of the ordeal. NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . article.description: La NASA seleccionó a tres empresas el miércoles para realizar trabajos de desarrollo de conceptos de capacidad de retransmisión
article.explanation: **NASA anuncia adjudicaciones de retransmisión satelital en banda Ka para comunicaciones espaciales** NASA ha seleccionado a tres empresas para desarrollar conceptos de capacidad de retransmisión espacial en banda Ka, asegurando la continuidad del servicio para las naves espaciales actuales sin necesidad de modificaciones en sus sistemas. Este anuncio se realizó el miércoles y forma parte del programa Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3. Las empresas adjudicatarias son Astranis Space Technologies Corp., que recibirá $264.3 millones; Global Enterprise Solutions Inc., con un contrato de $340.4 millones; y Viasat Inc., que obtendrá $460.9 millones. Estos contratos son de precio fijo y permiten a NASA la opción de financiar el avance desde el desarrollo inicial hasta una demostración de vuelo en órbita. El periodo inicial de ejecución se extiende desde el 4 de noviembre de 2026 hasta el 3 de mayo de 2027, con opciones adicionales para continuar el trabajo hasta 2029. Esta iniciativa es parte del programa SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) y busca reemplazar gradualmente la flota de satélites de seguimiento y datos, adoptando servicios comerciales para futuras misiones.

article.original_title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
article.source_body: Credit: NASA NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems. Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace. The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029. The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are: Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million. Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million. Viasat Inc. for $460.9 million. Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services. article.description: El súper tifón In-fa desarrolló un ojo inusualmente grande, y los remanentes del tifón Champi se transformaron en una tormenta extratropical que se dirigió a Alaska.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: La movida temporada de tormentas del Pacífico**

La temporada de tormentas en el Pacífico ha mostrado una actividad inusualmente alta desde abril de 2026, cuando el tifón Sinlaku alcanzó la categoría de supertifón y causó estragos en Micronesia, Guam y las Islas Marianas del Norte. Hasta finales de octubre, se han registrado 25 tormentas nombradas, destacando el Super Tifón In-fa, que se encontraba activo cerca de las Islas Marianas el 29 de octubre.

In-fa es el quinto tifón que afecta a las Islas Marianas este año y se caracteriza por su forma casi circular y un gran ojo, lo que lo clasifica como una tormenta anular, un fenómeno raro que representa solo el 4% de los ciclones tropicales en el noroeste del Pacífico. Estas tormentas tienden a mantener su intensidad durante más tiempo, incluso en condiciones desfavorables.

Por otro lado, los restos del tifón Champi se acercaron a Alaska, donde se reportaron vientos fuertes y lluvias intensas, aunque sin causar daños catastróficos. Este año, Alaska ha recibido cuatro ex-tifones, un fenómeno que se ha vuelto más común debido a un fuerte El Niño, que ha influido en la trayectoria de las tormentas, llevándolas hacia el norte en lugar de continuar su camino hacia Asia.

article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific Basin has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Twenty-five named storms later, the basin still hummed with activity in late October. When the EPIC (Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera) on the DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory) satellite captured this image (above) on October 29, 2026, Super Typhoon In-fa churned near the Mariana Islands. At the same time, the remnants of Typhoon Champi approached Alaska amid a parade of storms moving across the Bering Sea. In-fa is the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands this year. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured the image of In-fa below on October 30, when the storm was just west of the island chain. In-fa was unusually intense at the time of the image, with a nearly circular shape and large eye—a collection of characteristics that meteorologists use to identify a subset of tropical cyclones known as annular storms . These storms typically lack prominent outer spiral-shaped rainbands—a common feature of standard tropical cyclones—which is why meteorologists have a habit of calling annular storms “doughnuts” or “truck tires.” Annular storms are rare, accounting for just 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific, according to one analysis . Their eyes average about 45 kilometers (30 miles) in diameter, compared to about 25 kilometers for standard tropical cyclones, and the storms typically maintain their strength longer in unfavorable conditions. In-fa was still a tropical cyclone when EPIC captured the image at the top of the page, but Champi’s leftovers had gone through the process of extratropical transition and become a whole different type of storm as they entered the Bering Sea’s busy storm track. Tropical cyclones are warm-core storms fueled by the heat and moisture of warm ocean water, but extratropical cyclones typically have cold cores and draw energy from temperature contrasts between warm and cold air masses. Unlike tropical cyclones, extratropical cyclones typically develop fronts and huge, spiraling cloud bands shaped like commas . “One of the calling cards of extratropical transitions is the expansion of a storm’s wind field,” said Gary Partyka, a meteorologist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “It’s not that the winds necessarily grow stronger, but they cover a much larger area,” he said. In this case, there likely would still have been a midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, possibly with large, comma-shaped clouds on October 30, even without Champi’s remnants, he added. “But it looks like Champi became intertwined with and helped intensify that system,” he said. Champi’s transformation came after a long and destructive tour through the West Pacific, during which the typhoon achieved maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometers (185 miles) per hour, prompting some observers to call it one of the strongest storms of the season. Despite narrowly skirting Taiwan and Guam, the powerhouse storm brought damaging winds and intense rains to both places, as well as to parts of China and Japan. When the remnants hit Alaska, the state avoided catastrophic damage on the scale of what happened after ex-typhoon Halong struck in October 2025 , but some areas did see high winds and heavy rain and snowfall, according to news reports . Champi is the fourth ex-typhoon to enter Alaskan waters this year, noted University of Alaska Fairbanks meteorologist and climatologist Rick Thoman , following Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October. The autumns of 1997 and 2015—both very strong El Niño years—had three each, he added. Roughly 60 ex-typhoons have impacted the state since 1970 , according to Thoman. Partyka described 2026 as a “particularly active year” for Pacific tropical cyclones, increasing the chances that Alaska would be affected by storms that have gone through extratropical transitions. The strong El Niño underway in the Pacific is a “likely contributor” to the increased activity, he added. El Niño is a climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years, marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. In the Northwest Pacific, the phenomenon tends to cause storms to more readily curve northward rather than continuing westward to East Asia and Southeast Asia, some experts say , bringing more storms toward Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula. article.description: Los satélites de la NASA han capturado una inquietante formación en forma de calavera en una remota isla de la Antártida, pero su apariencia fantasmal oculta una preocupante advertencia sobre el derretimiento de los glaciares. Las temperaturas invernales inusualmente cálidas han expuesto grandes áreas de hielo oscuro, lo que podría acelerar el derretimiento futuro y transformar gradualmente las características fantasmales de la calavera.
article.explanation:
**NASA revela una inquietante calavera oculta en el hielo de la Antártica**

Ubicada en el Mar de Weddell, la Isla Vega presenta una apariencia inquietante que recuerda a una calavera. Este fenómeno visual es el resultado de formaciones naturales, como un nunatak que simula un ojo vacío y una moraine lateral que contornea la boca. Sin embargo, detrás de esta imagen se esconde una preocupación mayor: el estado cambiante de los glaciares antárticos.

Imágenes satelitales de la NASA muestran un notable cambio en la cobertura de nieve entre marzo de 2025 y octubre de 2026. En marzo, la isla estaba cubierta de nieve, pero para octubre, amplias secciones estaban expuestas, revelando hielo de glaciar más oscuro. Según el glaciólogo Mauri Pelto, las condiciones inusualmente cálidas durante el invierno de 2026 contribuyeron a esta pérdida de nieve, que se vio agravada por la sublimación y vientos fuertes.

La falta de nieve tiene consecuencias significativas. La nieve fresca refleja la luz solar, mientras que el hielo oscuro la absorbe, lo que podría acelerar el derretimiento de los glaciares. Aunque una delgada capa de nieve podría ralentizar temporalmente este proceso, la continua exposición del hielo podría transformar la apariencia de la isla, erosionando las formaciones que le dan su forma distintiva.

Rober, quien se unirá desde California, compartirá su experiencia como ingeniero de la NASA y creador de contenido, destacando la importancia de la curiosidad y la resolución de problemas.

Este evento también marca el inicio de una colaboración entre la NASA y la Fundación ClassCrunchLabs, con el objetivo de ampliar el acceso a experiencias de aprendizaje STEM. La iniciativa busca inspirar a más estudiantes a involucrarse en la ciencia y la ingeniería, preparándolos para futuras oportunidades en el sector aeroespacial y más allá.

article.description: Científicos que utilizan el Mars Express de la Agencia Espacial Europea, en combinación con un modelo meteorológico de última generación del Planeta Rojo, han descubierto que puede haber una física muy exótica detrás de la nube más curiosa de Marte.
article.explanation:
**La nube más rara de Marte podría ser incluso más rara de lo que pensábamos**

Científicos que utilizan la sonda Mars Express de la Agencia Espacial Europea han descubierto que la formación de la nube más curiosa de Marte, conocida como la Nube Alargada de Arsia Mons (AMEC), podría involucrar procesos físicos poco comunes. Esta nube, que aparece cada primavera y verano en el hemisferio sur del planeta rojo, se forma a partir de vapor de agua que se congela directamente en partículas de hielo, un fenómeno conocido como nucleación homogénea.

Tradicionalmente, se pensaba que las nubes se formaban a partir de la condensación de vapor de agua en presencia de partículas como polvo o sal. Sin embargo, en el caso de la AMEC, se ha observado que este proceso ocurre sin la necesidad de tales partículas, lo que es completamente inesperado y no se había documentado en otras atmósferas planetarias.

Los investigadores han determinado que la combinación de la delgada atmósfera de Marte y la altura del volcán Arsia Mons crea condiciones únicas que permiten este fenómeno. Al fluir el viento sobre el volcán, se generan ondas que elevan rápidamente el aire húmedo, provocando un enfriamiento drástico que permite la formación de la nube.

Este hallazgo no solo amplía nuestro entendimiento sobre la atmósfera marciana, sino que también sugiere que procesos inusuales podrían estar presentes en otros planetas del universo.

article.description: Los científicos han descubierto que el magma en el interior de la Tierra puede almacenar sorprendentes cantidades de oxígeno adicional, lo que podría revelar un contribuyente oculto a la atmósfera rica en oxígeno de nuestro planeta. Los hallazgos sugieren que antiguas erupciones volcánicas pueden haber ayudado a transformar la atmósfera de la Tierra hace miles de millones de años, con implicaciones para entender la vida en otros planetas.
article.explanation:
**Científicos descubren un reservorio de oxígeno oculto en las profundidades de la Tierra**

Investigadores han revelado que el magma en las profundidades de la Tierra puede almacenar mucho más oxígeno de lo que se pensaba anteriormente. Este hallazgo, liderado por el Dr. Yanhao Lin y el Dr. Ho-kwang Mao del Centro de Ciencia y Tecnología de Alta Presión (HPSTAR), desafía creencias arraigadas sobre la composición del magma y sugiere que el oxígeno liberado desde el interior del planeta pudo haber influido en la transformación de la atmósfera terrestre hace miles de millones de años.

A través de experimentos de alta presión y simulaciones computacionales, los científicos descubrieron que el magma puede absorber oxígeno adicional, más allá de lo que su composición química habitual permitiría. En condiciones extremas, como presiones de hasta 7 gigapascales y temperaturas entre 1200 y 1800 °C, se encontró que el oxígeno adicional podía representar más del 5% del peso de las muestras analizadas.

Este descubrimiento plantea interrogantes sobre el papel del magma en la historia de la Tierra, sugiriendo que podría haber transportado oxígeno desde el interior hacia la superficie, contribuyendo así a la oxidación de la atmósfera. Los investigadores estiman que, si el magma liberara solo el 0.27% de su peso en oxígeno, podría igualar la cantidad total de oxígeno presente en la atmósfera actual. Estos hallazgos podrían tener implicaciones significativas en la comprensión de la evolución atmosférica de la Tierra y otros planetas rocosos.

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: El Niño antes y ahora**

En octubre de 2026, los niveles del mar en el Pacífico ecuatorial central y oriental son más altos de lo normal, un fenómeno característico del evento de El Niño. Este patrón se asemeja al observado en octubre de 1997, durante uno de los eventos más intensos registrados en la historia de la altimetría satelital. Según datos de la NASA, la comparación entre ambos años muestra un aumento significativo en la temperatura del agua y la altura del nivel del mar.

El fenómeno de El Niño, que ocurre cada dos a siete años, trae consigo un calentamiento de las aguas del Pacífico, alterando patrones climáticos globales. Los eventos de 1997-98 y 2015-16 causaron estragos en diversas regiones, desde incendios en Indonesia hasta inundaciones en California. Actualmente, se prevé que el evento de 2026 sea comparable en magnitud a estos anteriores, con un 83% de probabilidad de que se mantenga fuerte hasta principios de 2027.

Josh Willis, científico del Laboratorio de Propulsión a Chorro de la NASA, advierte que, aunque el fenómeno actual presenta similitudes con el de 1997, cada evento tiene características únicas que pueden influir en sus impactos climáticos. La incertidumbre persiste, y se espera que los efectos de El Niño se sientan en diversas partes del mundo, incluyendo Chile, donde podrían intensificarse las lluvias y afectar la agricultura.

El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years, bringing warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific. The most recent very strong El Niño events, in 1997-98 and 2015-16, upended weather patterns. Impacts spanned the planet, from fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, to crop failures due to drought in southern Africa , to heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California. The current El Niño rivals these past heavyweights. Every El Niño grows from a feedback loop between the atmosphere and the ocean. Trade winds normally keep warm water piled up in the western Pacific, where it stands higher than in the east. When those winds weaken, that warm water begins to pulse eastward, which further weakens and sometimes reverses the winds, allowing even more warm water to move east. The cycle intensifies as waters continue to warm and pile up in the central and eastern Pacific. But each El Niño has its own character, shaped by where in the Pacific the warmth builds and how the atmosphere responds. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.” Altimetry satellites can track those differences by measuring the height of the sea surface. Because water expands as it warms, higher-than-normal sea levels in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific signal the buildup of heat associated with El Niño. The maps above depict sea surface height anomalies across the Pacific Ocean on October 13, 1997 (left), and on October 12, 2026 (right). Data are from the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite and the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite, respectively, and were processed by scientists at JPL. Shades of red indicate where sea levels were higher than average. Normal sea level conditions appear white, and lower areas are blue. Signals related to seasonal cycles and long-term trends have been removed to highlight sea level anomalies associated with El Niño and other short-term natural phenomena. “What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.” Compared with the 1997-98 event, El Niño in 2026 came on much more suddenly. But as of October, the two events appear similar in character—the tilt of sea level (low in the west and high in the east) and high, warm water extending all the way to South America—so Willis thinks the impacts could be similar as well. In 1997-98, that meant, for instance, lots of rain in California and across the southern tier of the U.S. The 2015-16 El Niño was also very strong, as elevated sea levels in October 2015 (middle) show. But its pattern differed from those in October 1997 (top) and October 2026 (bottom): less of the elevated water reached the coast of South America, which contributed to different weather patterns that year. The 2015-16 El Niño was another heavy hitter but differed in its character. Sea surface height anomalies on October 12, 2015, based on altimetry data from the Jason-2 satellite, are shown above in context with maps from around the same time in 1997 and 2026. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator didn’t push up against South America to the extent it did in the other years. Rainfall impacts that winter concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern U.S., with significant flooding in Mexico. NOAA’s El Niño outlook on October 8, 2026, called for an 83 percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño through the first three months of 2027. But exactly how the impacts will play out in winter 2026-27 and beyond remains to be seen. article.description: Profundamente bajo la caldera Kikai de Japón, un masivo reservorio de magma se está reabasteciendo 7,300 años después de una de las erupciones volcánicas más poderosas en la reciente historia geológica de la Tierra. Los científicos utilizaron encuestas sísmicas submarinas para revelar un vasto almacén de magma que parece haberse acumulado desde la antigua catástrofe. El descubrimiento podría ayudar a explicar cómo los supervolcanes como Yellowstone y Toba reconstruyen sus suministros de magma.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Uno de los supervolcanes más poderosos de la Tierra se está rellenando con magma fresco**

Investigadores de la Universidad de Kobe han descubierto que el supervolcán Kikai, ubicado en Japón, está acumulando magma fresco en su enorme reservorio subterráneo, miles de años después de una de las erupciones más devastadoras de la historia geológica reciente. Esta erupción ocurrió hace aproximadamente 7,300 años y fue la más grande del Holoceno.

El estudio, publicado en Communications Earth & Environment, revela que el magma actual no es simplemente material residual de la erupción anterior. Se ha identificado un nuevo domo de lava en desarrollo en el centro de la caldera, lo que sugiere que el magma proviene de inyecciones recientes de roca fundida desde las profundidades de la corteza terrestre. Los investigadores utilizaron técnicas sísmicas avanzadas para mapear el reservorio, encontrando una región significativa con alta proporción de magma justo debajo del sitio de la erupción histórica.

Este hallazgo no indica que una nueva erupción sea inminente, sino que proporciona una visión crucial sobre cómo los supervolcanes pueden recargar sus reservas de magma a lo largo de miles de años. Comprender este proceso es vital para anticipar el comportamiento de otros supervolcanes, como Yellowstone y Toba.

article.explanation:
**El asteroide mató a los dinosaurios. ¿Por qué sobrevivieron los cocodrilos?**

Un nuevo estudio sugiere que la preferencia de los cocodrilos por ambientes cálidos les otorgó una ventaja crucial durante la extinción masiva que acabó con los dinosaurios hace 66 millones de años. Investigadores de University College London analizaron más de 7,000 fósiles y registros de más de 400 especies, tanto vivas como extintas, para entender cómo los cocodrilos y sus parientes sobrevivieron a este evento catastrófico.

Los resultados indican que, tras el impacto del asteroide, las regiones tropicales y subtropicales continuaron siendo adecuadas para los parientes de los cocodrilos, a diferencia de muchos dinosaurios que vieron deteriorar sus hábitats. Las simulaciones climáticas sugieren que áreas cercanas al ecuador pudieron haber mantenido temperaturas cálidas, proporcionando refugios esenciales para las poblaciones sobrevivientes.

Además, se identificaron características que podrían haber mejorado las posibilidades de supervivencia de los cocodrilos, como su tamaño relativamente pequeño, la capacidad de vivir parcialmente en el agua y sus modestos requerimientos energéticos. Este estudio no solo arroja luz sobre la historia evolutiva de los cocodrilos, sino que también plantea interrogantes sobre cómo responderán a los cambios climáticos actuales, dado que la urbanización y la agricultura limitan su movilidad hacia hábitats adecuados.

Las zonas de subducción son áreas donde una placa tectónica se desliza por debajo de otra, y su estudio es crucial para entender los procesos geológicos que ocurren en el fondo marino.

La desintegración de esta placa oceánica ofrece una oportunidad única para investigar cómo estas zonas pueden cambiar con el tiempo y qué implica su "muerte" en términos geológicos. Este tipo de investigación es fundamental para ampliar nuestro conocimiento sobre la dinámica de la Tierra y los procesos que afectan la formación y destrucción de las placas tectónicas.

article.description: Una erupción volcánica catastrófica hace 7.300 años devastó Japón, pero una
article.explanation: Una masiva erupción volcánica que golpeó Japón hace unos 7,300 años tuvo un impacto devastador en las comunidades prehistóricas, pero sus consecuencias fueron mucho más complicadas de lo que los científicos creían anteriormente. Mientras que algunas poblaciones disminuyeron o desaparecieron de las áreas afectadas, otras continuaron creciendo a pesar de la destrucción. Un equipo de investigación internacional liderado por la Universidad de Lund investigó cómo la erupción Kikai-Akahoya cambió los patrones de población en Japón. Sus hallazgos desafían la idea de que el desastre o bien aniquiló completamente a las comunidades cercanas o las dejó en gran medida sin afectar. En cambio, los investigadores descubrieron una sorprendente mezcla de disminución de la población, migración, adaptación y crecimiento. Cuando el volcán Kikai-Akahoya erupcionó bajo el mar aproximadamente hace 7,300 años, Japón era hogar de comunidades Jomon que dependían de la caza y la recolección para sobrevivir. "Esta erupción debió ser devastadora, explotando desde el lecho marino con poca advertencia. Golpeó las islas japonesas con poderosos terremotos y enormes tsunamis, y luego cubrió el paisaje con metros de ceniza volcánica", explica el autor principal Peter Jordan, profesor de arqueología en la Universidad de Lund.

**TITULAR: NASA comparte planes para acelerar Artemis y volver a la Luna.**

**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

NASA ha presentado un ambicioso plan para acelerar su programa Artemis, con el objetivo de llevar a astronautas estadounidenses de regreso a la Luna en 2028. En una actualización realizada el 23 de octubre, el administrador de la agencia, Jared Isaacman, destacó los avances hacia la misión Artemis III, programada para 2027, y la misión Artemis IV, que se llevará a cabo un año después.

La misión Artemis III incluirá el envío de cuatro astronautas a la órbita terrestre baja para probar sistemas críticos necesarios para futuros aterrizajes lunares. Este vuelo se realizará a bordo de la nave Orion, lanzada por el cohete Space Launch System (SLS). La misión también contempla la colaboración con SpaceX y Blue Origin para el desarrollo de vehículos de aterrizaje lunar.

Además, NASA ha reducido a la mitad los plazos de procesamiento de hardware para Artemis III y ha desarrollado internamente un componente crítico de la línea de combustible a un costo significativamente menor. Para la misión Artemis IV, se están considerando dos opciones de etapa superior para el SLS, lo que garantiza flexibilidad en la ejecución de la misión.

Con estos esfuerzos, NASA busca establecer una presencia humana sostenible en la Luna y sentar las bases para futuras misiones a Marte.

article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028. Agency leadership provided updates on the previously announced acceleration plans for the Artemis program, advancing toward the agency’s Artemis III test flight in 2027 and Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028. Building on the priorities announced at Ignition earlier this year, NASA leadership shared the agency’s significant progress across its missions, working with industry partners to test critical capabilities, reduce risk, and build toward a sustained American presence on the Moon. This graphic shows NASA’s concept of operations for Artemis III. The mission will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit next year to test critical systems needed for future lunar landings. NASA “This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible,” said Isaacman. “NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we’re not waiting for others to bring their plans to us — the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth.” The agency shared details of the Artemis III mission, which will test rendezvous, docking, and operations between NASA’s Orion spacecraft and lunar lander test vehicles from SpaceX and Blue Origin in Earth orbit. Four astronauts will fly aboard Orion, launched on NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit to reduce risk ahead of the Artemis IV moon landing mission. The Artemis III mission will unfold in sequence: Blue Origin will launch a Blue Moon lander test article into Earth orbit, SLS will launch Orion and its crew, docking with the Blue Moon lander test article, then SpaceX will launch a Version 3 Starship lander test article while Orion will undock from Blue Moon and dock with Starship. The Oct. 23 updates follow other recent updates about the Artemis missions. Hardware for Artemis III is on track, with processing timelines sharply reduced by about half. NASA also redesigned, built, and tested a critical fuel-line component in-house in five months, at roughly a tenth of the cost of an earlier outside-vendor estimate. “NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it,” said Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager. “It’s an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise.” Artemis IV: Pursuing multiple paths to Moon landing For the agency’s Artemis IV mission in 2028, astronauts will launch aboard Orion on the SLS rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop lunar landers to carry those astronauts to the Moon’s surface. Both companies have redesigned their approaches to simplify the missions and make them more efficient and flexible as compared to previous mission designs. SpaceX’s Starship will refuel in Earth orbit, rendezvous with Orion, and then carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Blue Origin’s approach involves transfer stages in Earth orbit to push its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander toward the Moon, where it will meet Orion in a closer lunar orbit before descending to the surface. NASA NASA Both SpaceX and Blue Origin are targeting to be able to support a crewed lunar landing in 2028. For Artemis IV, NASA is pursuing two upper-stage options for the SLS rocket: its current stage, the interim cryogenic propulsion stage; and a stretched version of ULA’s Centaur V which can carry more propellant. Pursuing both options ensures NASA is maintaining flexibility and preventing single-point dependency. NASA also announced plans with spacesuit provider Axiom Space to develop a second, lighter suit design called the “Sortie suit” to enable the first moonwalks. The Sortie suit will not replace Axiom’s primary suit, which will be used for longer, more demanding missions in the future. The Sortie suit is roughly half the weight of the larger suit and lets NASA move faster on the earliest surface missions. As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions at the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars. **TITULAR: NASA presenta el avión experimental X-70 para impulsar la investigación en aviación**

NASA ha revelado su nuevo avión experimental, el X-70 Fractal, durante el UP.Summit en el Centro Espacial Kennedy en Florida, el pasado miércoles. Este innovador avión, diseñado como una plataforma de investigación altamente adaptable, tiene como objetivo acelerar el desarrollo y la prueba de tecnologías avanzadas en aviación.

El X-70, que cuenta con un peso de despegue de 10,000 libras, es capaz de alcanzar velocidades de crucero de Mach 0.75 y altitudes de hasta 45,000 pies. Además, puede transportar hasta 2,000 libras de carga experimental, lo que le permite realizar una amplia gama de investigaciones y pruebas de vuelo. Jared Isaacman, administrador de NASA, destacó que esta plataforma permitirá explorar la maniobrabilidad de las aeronaves de maneras nunca antes vistas en vuelos tripulados.

Se espera que el X-70 realice su primer vuelo bajo la bandera de NASA en los próximos dos años. Este nuevo avión se suma a una larga tradición de aeronaves experimentales que han contribuido a establecer el liderazgo de Estados Unidos en el ámbito de la aviación, desde el Bell X-1 hasta el X-59. Con el X-70, NASA busca expandir su capacidad para realizar investigaciones de vuelo experimentales y avanzar en la próxima generación de aviación estadounidense.

article.source_body: Generated image of NASA’s new X-70 Fractal experimental aircraft, a crewed, rapidly reconfigurable research platform for advanced aviation technologies. On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies. The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities. “The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.” The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions. “For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.” The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America’s leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight. With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation. article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Ciclón Arnab Devasta la Costa Este de India**

El ciclón Arnab, la primera tormenta nombrada de la temporada de ciclones del Océano Índico Norte 2026, se formó en la Bahía de Bengala el 25 de octubre. Con vientos sostenidos de hasta 140 kilómetros por hora, el fenómeno meteorológico tocó tierra en la costa de Andhra Pradesh y Yanam el 28 de octubre, donde se registraron vientos de 130 kilómetros por hora, clasificándose como un "ciclón muy severo" según el Departamento Meteorológico de India (IMD).

La tormenta impactó entre Bapatla y Visakhapatnam, una región densamente poblada que alberga grandes ciudades y comunidades pesqueras. Arnab causó daños extensos, derribando árboles, inundando cultivos y hogares, y afectando las operaciones pesqueras y las redes de transporte y energía. Las autoridades indias evacuaron a más de 84,000 personas de áreas costeras vulnerables antes de la llegada del ciclón.

Este evento se produce en el contexto de un fenómeno de El Niño, que altera las condiciones oceánicas y puede influir en la actividad ciclónica. A pesar de que se espera una reducción en la frecuencia e intensidad de los ciclones durante años de El Niño, Arnab ha demostrado ser una excepción significativa, dejando a su paso un saldo de al menos tres víctimas fatales y una devastación considerable en la región.

article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Arnab Strikes India Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search The first named storm of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season—Arnab (pronounced Or-nab)—emerged in the Bay of Bengal on October 25, a rather late start for a basin that typically produces named cyclones in April or May. When the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-20 captured this nighttime image at 20:12 Universal Time on October 26 (1:42 a.m. India Standard Time on October 27), the storm had sustained winds of about 140 kilometers (85 miles) per hour, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). When Arnab made landfall on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early on October 28, sustained winds were 130 kilometers per hour. IMD categorizes a storm that strength as a “very severe cyclonic storm ,” which is similar to a Category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale . It made landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, a heavily settled area home to large cities, farmland, and fishing communities. Arnab caused extensive damage, uprooting trees, inundating crops and homes, limiting fishing operations, and disrupting transportation and power networks, according to news reports . Prior to landfall, Indian authorities had evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas. The storm comes in the midst of an El Niño , a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific that emerges roughly every two to seven years. The changed ocean conditions can influence the atmosphere in ways that alter global weather patterns and change the distribution of rainfall, winds, tropical cyclones, fires, floods, and other phenomena. In the Bay of Bengal, for instance, some research indicates that altered environmental conditions during an El Niño are associated with a reduction in tropical cyclone activity. The ocean basin sees both less frequent and less intense tropical cyclones during El Niño years, researchers have found. The orbital outpost was soaring 263 miles above the Indian Ocean, off the coast of Madagascar, at the time of this photograph. Credit: NASA Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA. The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25. Liftoff is targeted for no earlier than 10:49 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following launch, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture Cygnus and install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. The spacecraft will remain at the space station until May 2027. This is the company’s 25th spacecraft built to deliver supplies to the International Space Station under contract with NASA. Credentialing to cover prelaunch and launch activities is open to U.S. media. The application deadline for U.S. citizens is 11:59 p.m. EST, Thursday, Nov. 12. All accreditation requests must be submitted online at: https://media.ksc.nasa.gov Credentialed media will receive a confirmation email following approval. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online. For questions about accreditation, or to request special logistical support, email: ksc-media-accreditat@mail.nasa.gov. For other questions, please contact NASA’s Kennedy Space Center newsroom at: 321-867-2468. In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles in space that could improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, as well as a study that could guide cancer treatments by predicting whether a patient’s cancer is likely to spread to other parts of the body. Cygnus also will carry human muscle cells and medications to test therapeutics for muscle loss associated with spaceflight and aging on Earth, and a compact radiation sensor designed to improve crew safety on future missions. Each resupply mission to the station delivers scientific investigations in the areas of biology and biotechnology, Earth and space science, physical sciences, and technology development and demonstrations. Cargo resupply from U.S. companies ensures a national capability to deliver scientific research to the space station, increasing NASA’s ability to conduct new investigations aboard humanity’s laboratory in space. For 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs that are not possible on Earth. The space station is an important testbed for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of long-duration spaceflight and to expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. As commercial companies concentrate on providing human space transportation services and destinations as part of a strong low Earth orbit economy , NASA is focusing its resources on deep space missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs to build on our foundation for the first astronaut missions to Mars.
